type.name: Feature
type.description: A request, idea, or new functionality

candidates.body:
### Feature request

Hi, we are big fans of the library and the NF4 data-type, so much so that we have been working on [CUDA kernels](https://github.com/HanGuo97/flute) to speed-up inference for NF4-quantized models (and more). We'd love to explore ways we can integrate FLUTE into the `bitsandbytes` library.

### Motivation

I think FLUTE could make two contributions to bitsandbytes:

- An inference-time kernel for NF4-quantized LLM (and more). For example, this could help extend the current GEMV kernel into GEMM (i.e., batched inference).
- A new quantization algorithm that lightly extends bitsandbytes's NF4 into a learned version.

The kernel and algorithm still have room for improvements. For example, it has limited GPU support, and specializes in specific shapes. These are hopefully not hard limits and could be relaxed. As such, we do not expect FLUTE to be the default option. That being said, we thought it'd be great to have FLUTE be an opt-in feature.

### Your contribution

We are happy to submit PRs, though I'm sure there will be some rough edges that we will need some help with.

candidates.title: [RFC] Extend bitsandbytes to support Intel hardware platforms

labels.name: RFC
labels.description: request for comments on proposed library improvements

candidates.body:
# Motivation

The current bitsandbytes library is bound with the CUDA platforms. However, we are seeing that there is a rapidly growing demand to run large language models (LLMs) on more platforms like Intel® CPUs and GPUs devices ("xpu" is the device tag for Intel GPU in PyTorch). Therefore, we aim at extending Intel® CPU and GPU ecosystem support and optimizations to bitsandbytes and offer the same scope of the lower-precision computation features (8bits and 4bits) as CUDA.

# Approach
To provide the 8bits and 4bits features for Intel platforms, we propose two major changes as follows:

1. A device abstraction that allows non-CUDA devices to be added to bitsandbytes easily. It contains a device backend abstraction that contains the key kernel interfaces to implement by each backend, a backend registration interface to add new device backends, and a kernel dispatching mechanism.
2. Lightweight enabling of Intel CPU and GPU support on top of the device abstraction. We plan to leverage the PyTorch 2.x compiler stack and the custom kernels provided by Intel Extension for PyTorch (IPEX) to support Intel CPU and GPU without the needs of upstreaming native backend codes. This reduces the complexity of adding new devices to bitsandbytes and also reduces maintenance costs.

## Device abstraction
We will extend CUDA dependency to Intel CPU/GPU in bitsandbytes device setup and init. We will provide common device abstractions for general devices (there will be no changes on CUDA).
Note that there is also no API or usage change for Huggingface users to use different devices with bitsandbytes.
```python
from transformers import BitsAndBytesConfig
nf4_config = BitsAndBytesConfig(
   load_in_4bit=True,
   bnb_4bit_quant_type="nf4",
   bnb_4bit_use_double_quant=True,
   bnb_4bit_compute_dtype=torch.bfloat16,
)
model_nf4 = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(model_id, quantization_config=nf4_config)
```

## Lightweight integration for Intel CPU/GPU
We will do lightweight and simple integration to enable low-precision computation features, both 8bits and 4bits. We don't plan to add native backend code for Intel CPU and GPU in the first step. Instead, we employ PyTorch 2.x compilation and Intel® Extension for PyTorch to enable those features.

- For performance-critical functions, such as GEMM, we will import IPEX as a Python module and use its API for computation. IPEX can provide the best performance for such functions across Intel devices (for example by adopting the 4th generation of Intel® Xeon® Scalable Processors with Intel® Advanced Matrix Extensions instruction set).
  - IPEX, as the speedup optional component, has already been integrated into Huggingface mainstream functionality tools like the Trainer Class and the accelerate repo to speed up training and inference. Similar to Huggingface, we will also integrate IPEX with bitsandbytes as a Python library dependency.

For example:
```python
import intel_extension_for_pytorch
def cpu/xpu_igemmlt(*args, **kwargs):
    # Staff before computation
    C_i32 = torch.ops.torch_ipex.matmul_i8i8i32(A_i8, B_i8)  # GEMM computaion
    # Other staff
```

- For other functions, we adopt the PyTorch 2.x compilation technology. We will implement them using PyTorch basic operators in Python and optimize the functions using [torch.compile](https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.compile.html) to get good performance. Intel is one of the major contributors to the torch.compile CPU backend  in PyTorch and also hosted the torch.compile GPU backend in IPEX. The implementation can also work for other devices that support the PyTorch 2.x compiler stack.

For example:
```python
@torch.compile
def double_quant_cpu/xpu(*args, **kwargs):
    # Implement double_quant for Intel CPU/GPU with PyTorch ops
    # torch.compile will generate kernel code and compile at runtime
```


# Design

## (1) Reorganize device_setup to support multiple devices

_Intel CPU or GPU_
1. is_ipex_available
2. import IPEX OPs (and also check Intel GPU device availability)

_CUDA_
1. Remain the same, load from lib_cuda.so

![1](https://github.com/TimDettmers/bitsandbytes/assets/83276252/837b1131-f0c3-4291-8be3-5220e22135df)

## (2) Device backend abstraction with key kernel interfaces
Key functions that are used in mainstream 8bits and 4bits:

- Performance-critical:

| F.igemmlt |

- Others:

| F.double_quant| F.mm_dequant| F.transform| F.extract_outliers| F.quantize_4bit| F.dequantize_4bit |

To extend the support of the above functions on Intel CPU/GPU (CUDA remains the same), we propose the following designs:
![2](https://github.com/TimDettmers/bitsandbytes/assets/83276252/7b94577b-092c-463a-9414-3e7fe8aa399e)

# PR plans:

- [x] Enable device abstraction for Intel CPU/GPU and CUDA
       Adding options of init Intel CPU/GPU device but no implementations, CUDA remains the same.
- [ ] Enable 8bits functionality for Intel CPU/GPU
       Adding implementations of 8bits functions for Intel CPU/GPU devices.
- [ ] Enable 4bits functionality for Intel CPU/GPU
       Adding implementations of 4bits functions for Intel CPU/GPU devices.

# Additional contents
Besides, we will also propose the PR to Transformers upstream to extend the usage of bitsandbytes API on multi-devices.

**Transformers changes**
- _bitsandbytes_available 
- Not limited to CUDA devices available
- Use CUDA/CPU and Intel GPU device [here](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/blob/main/src/transformers/integrations/bitsandbytes.py#L95-L98)

![3](https://github.com/TimDettmers/bitsandbytes/assets/83276252/cb0e7dee-9831-4f09-9a93-2ef390204a8f)

candidates.title: [RFC]Add x86 CPU support

labels.name: RFC
labels.description: request for comments on proposed library improvements

candidates.body:
## Summary    
Add x86 CPU support for low-bit training and inference.  

## Motivation
The current bitsandbytes library is bound with CUDA environment. We are seeing that there is a growing demand to run LLMs on CPU devices.

We experimented weight-only 4 bits and 8 bits GEMMs on multiple ISAs such as AVX512_F, AVX512_VNNI, and AMX_INT8, and demonstrated decent performance on x86 CPUs. We would like to contribute these kernels to bitsandbytes and make LLMs more accessible as CPUs are more ubiquitous.
## Proposed Implementation
We plan a two-phase support on x86 CPU.

### Phase 1: enable CPU NF4 and FP4 kernels on bitsandbytes
In this phase, we may modify the existing Makefile to add our cpp and c files to cpuonly build target. We will seek minimum change of existing codes, especially the interface functions. For CUDA-only python functions, we will add CPU code path as quantize_blockwise. 
~~~bash
FILES_CPP := $(CSRC)/common.cpp $(CSRC)/cpu_ops.cpp $(CSRC)/pythonInterface.c ourfiles.cpp ourfiles.c

cpuonly: $(BUILD_DIR) env
	$(GPP) -std=c++14 -shared -fPIC -I $(ROOT_DIR)/csrc -I $(ROOT_DIR)/include $(FILES_CPP) -o ./bitsandbytes/libbitsandbytes_cpu.so
~~~

Our kernels will be integrated into bitsandbytes and make bitsandbytes become cross-platform (gpu and cpu). In the first stage, we would like to enable CPU training and inference on NF4 and FP4. To support both training and inference, we will add the CPU version quant, dequant, and 4bit_inference kernels.   

We will start our support with high-level ISAs above AVX512, like AVX512_F,  AVX512_VNNI, AMX_BF16, and AMX_INT8. These ISAs will allow CPU kernels to be executed on Intel cascade-lake, ice-lake, sapphire-rapid, and AMD genoa CPU series.   

Our kernel codes will be integrated as a header-only cpp library like cutlass. We will add some C-style functions for calling our kernels under the else branch of BUILD_CUDA in pythoninterface.c.

~~~cpp
#if BUILD_CUDA
//existing CUDA kernels
#else
//CPU kernels
//e.g.
void cquantize_blockwise_cpu_fp32_fp4(float * code, float  *A, float *absmax, unsigned char *out, int blocksize, const int n);
void cquantize_blockwise_cpu_fp32_nf4(float * code, float  *A, float *absmax, unsigned char *out, int blocksize, const int n);
//...
#endif
~~~


### Phase 2: add more CPU kernels 
In this phase, we may add more CPU kernels that may be needed by LLM training or inference. As we can see many CUDA kernels in the csrc folder, we understand there can be a lot of work for CPU implementation. But we have to admit that not all these GPU kernels are also valuable to CPUs. For example, CPUs' fp32 and fp16 compute capability is much lower than GPU devices, while bf16’s capability is closer to GPU’s. So we would like to implement more kernels that are valuable to CPUs.

candidates.title: enhancement: Add 4-bit quantization / inference support
candidates.body:
https://mobile.twitter.com/Tim_Dettmers/status/1605209177919750147
"Our analysis is extensive, spanning 5 models (BLOOM, BLOOM, Pythia, GPT-2, OPT), from 3 to 8-bit precision, and from 19M to 66B scale. We find the same result again and again: bit-level scaling improves from 16-bit to 4-bit precision but reverses at 3-bit precision."
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/5949853/223333001-8c406be3-9a30-4b0b-a604-49bb07c8bcf3.png)

-----------
According to [the case for 4-bit precision paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.09720) there are essentially only upsides to 4-bit quantization. Performance per bit goes up, speed (in some cases) goes up, and performance per parameter stays around the same, just as with 8-bit. 

There are already bleeding edge 4-bit quantization efforts such as [GPTQ for LLaMA](https://github.com/qwopqwop200/GPTQ-for-LLaMa)
> [GPTQ](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.17323) is currently the SOTA one shot quantization method for LLMs. GPTQ supports amazingly low 3-bit and 4-bit weight quantization. And it can be applied to LLaMa. I've actually confirmed that this works well in LLaMa 7b. I haven't tested the memory usage(n-bit cuda kernel), but I think it should work.
> 
> Model([LLaMa-7B](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.13971))	Bits	group-size	Wikitext2	PTB	C4
> FP16	16	-	5.67	8.79	7.05
> RTN	4	-	6.28	9.68	7.70
> [GPTQ](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.17323)	4	64	**6.16**	**9.66**	**7.52**
> RTN	3	-	25.66	61.25	28.19
> [GPTQ](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.17323)	3	64	**12.24**	**16.77**	**9.55**
> code: https://github.com/qwopqwop200/GPTQ-for-LLaMa
From: https://github.com/oobabooga/text-generation-webui/issues/177

Unfortunately these efforts are only academic PoC and are not useful for inference. 

-----------
Bitsandbytes is already used by many projects for its 8-bit implementation. By adding 4-bit these and other projects could benefit the same as they do now, except doubly so. Smaller models, more model accessibility, and better performance.

candidates.title: [Question] How to obtain the 4-bit inference speedup?

labels.name: High Priority
labels.description: (first issues that will be worked on)

candidates.body:
I tested the inference speed of LLaMa-7B with bitsandbutes-0.40 on A100-80G. I fonud that the speed of `nf4` has been greatly improved thah Qlora. However, the speed of `nf4` is still slower than `fp16`.

I conducted an inference speed test on LLaMa-7B using bitsandbytes-0.40 with A100-80G. I found that the speed of `nf4` has been significantly improved compared to Qlora. However, the speed of `nf4` is still slower than` fp16`.

Specifically, I evaluated the speed with the following code:
```
import torch
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer,BitsAndBytesConfig
import time
import pdb

MAX_NEW_TOKENS = 128
model_name = 'path/to/llama-7b'

text = 'Hamburg is in which country?\n'
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_name,use_fast=False)
input_ids = tokenizer(text, return_tensors="pt").input_ids
input_ids = input_ids.cuda()

free_in_GB = int(torch.cuda.mem_get_info()[0]/1024**3)
max_memory = f'{int(torch.cuda.mem_get_info()[0]/1024**3)-2}GB'

n_gpus = torch.cuda.device_count()
max_memory = {i: max_memory for i in range(n_gpus)}

model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
  model_name,
  device_map='auto',
  max_memory=max_memory,
)
time_1 = time.time()
num = 0
for i in range(5):
  generated_ids = model.generate(input_ids, max_length=MAX_NEW_TOKENS)
  num += len(generated_ids[0])

print(f"fp16 speed: {num/(time.time() - time_1)}token/s")

model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
  model_name,
  device_map='auto',
  load_in_4bit=True,
  max_memory=max_memory,
  quantization_config=BitsAndBytesConfig(
            load_in_4bit=True,
            bnb_4bit_compute_dtype=torch.bfloat16,
            bnb_4bit_use_double_quant=True,
            bnb_4bit_quant_type='nf4'
        ),
)
time_1 = time.time()
num = 0
for i in range(5):
  generated_ids = model.generate(input_ids, max_length=MAX_NEW_TOKENS)
  num += len(generated_ids[0])
print(f"nf4 speed: {num/(time.time() - time_1)}token/s")
```
the output is:
```
fp16 speed: 36.28083223507306token/s
nf4 speed: 21.665383178407968token/s
```
The above results show that `nf4` is only approximately `0.6x` the speed of `fp16`. I would like to know how to achieve the claimed `3.4x` speedup as mentioned in [this link](https://github.com/TimDettmers/bitsandbytes/releases/tag/0.40.0).

candidates.title: Inaccurate quantization with block sizes above 1024

labels.name: High Priority
labels.description: (first issues that will be worked on)

candidates.body:
# Bug description

Quantizing tensors with blocksize 1024 or more produces unexpectedly high errors.

For example:
```python
def debug_blocksize(block):
    x = torch.randn(4096, 4096).cuda()
    qx, qstate = F.quantize_fp4(x, blocksize=block)
    dq = F.dequantize_fp4(qx, qstate)
    return torch.sum(torch.linalg.norm(x - dq, ord="fro"))

for block in [64, 128, 256, 512, 1024, 2048]:
    print(debug_blocksize(block))
```

Results:
```
tensor(499.5332)
tensor(526.7997)
tensor(551.3618)
tensor(574.8427)
tensor(3437.5259)
tensor(3478.5842)
```

# Environment

- `bitsandbytes==0.39.1` installed with PyPI
- `python -m bitsandbytes`:

```
CUDA SETUP: Highest compute capability among GPUs detected: 7.5
CUDA SETUP: Detected CUDA version 118
CUDA SETUP: Loading binary /usr/local/lib/python3.10/dist-packages/bitsandbytes/libbitsandbytes_cuda118.so...
```

# Possible cause

I have compared the usage of `F.quantize`/`F.dequantize` with a manual fake implementation in Python to confirm that the library indeed gives results which are unexpected:

```python
def pivot_quant(qx, pivots, values):
    pivots = pivots.tolist()
    values = values.tolist()

    qx = torch.where(qx >= pivots[0], values[0], qx)
    for i in range(0, len(pivots) - 1):
      qx = torch.where(torch.logical_and(qx >= pivots[i+1], qx < pivots[i]), values[i+1], qx)
    qx = torch.where(qx <= pivots[-1], values[-1], qx)

    return qx

def setup_absmax_quant(inp, block):
    x = inp.view(-1, block)
    abs_max = torch.abs(x).max(dim=1,keepdim=True).values

    sign = torch.clamp(torch.sign(x)*2 + 1, -1, 1) # TODO: FIX
    qx = torch.abs(x) / abs_max
    return qx, abs_max, sign

def manual_e2m1(inp, block=64):
    qx, abs_max, sign = setup_absmax_quant(inp, block)

    # Exactly matching the fp4 implementation (E2M1)
    values = torch.tensor([12, 8, 6, 4, 3, 2, 0.0625, 0])
    pivots = torch.tensor([20, 14, 10, 7, 5, 2.0625, 0.0625]) / 2 / torch.max(values)
    qx = pivot_quant(qx, pivots, values) * sign

    dqx = qx / torch.max(values) * abs_max
    return dqx.view(inp.size())
```

Re-running the above experiment (here's a reproducible [Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/drive/14yzTJXGUjdt0KHECr6l_pvJWeuQ7lYkm?usp=sharing)) gives the following values:
```
(manual_e2m1, bnb_fp4)
(tensor(499.6785), tensor(499.6785))
(tensor(526.4285), tensor(526.4285))
(tensor(551.4703), tensor(551.4703))
(tensor(575.3717), tensor(575.3717))
(tensor(598.6218), tensor(3439.8052))
(tensor(622.5399), tensor(3482.6340))
```

Hi!
I'm trying to fine-tune LLama3-8B on a summarization dataset of about 1500 instances. The dataset contains long documents, often over 8K tokens. _Expected Memory usage:
Full-finetuning with FSDP needs ~16X80GB GPUs
FSDP + LoRA needs ~8X80GB GPUs
FSDP + Q-Lora needs ~2x40GB GPUs
FSDP + Q-Lora + CPU offloading needs 4x24GB GPUs, with 22 GB/GPU and 127 GB CPU RAM with a sequence length of 3072 and a batch size of 1.

```
As you can see, it seems that during the backward pass, the model runs out of memory. I find this pretty odd as I (should/probably) have enough GPU memory to accomodate for the 8B FSDP and QLORA setup.

### Possible limitations

CPU has too little ram. The offloading isn't possible because we only have 16GB of CPU ram. But following Phil Schmid's guide and not offloading to the CPU would suffice still, as we use 4 A40's. This is even more odd when you think that I'm using an 8B version, instead of the 70B versions that are used in both guides.

Not using Flash Attention 2 could also be an issue, but as seen in Phil Schmid's guide, SDPA can also be used.

Sequence length is too long, causing OOM. I tried setting the max_sequence_length to 512, but this didn't have any impact on the OOM issue.

### Caveat

I could see that the GPU memory was utilized pretty well and all GPU's were utilized up until 40GB or so. Because this took quite long, I wanted to use QLORA. But I couldn't just use QLORA device_map ='auto' together. That's why I resorted to FSDP in combination with QLORA. 

I don't really know why using QLORA in combination with FSDP would then result in the OOM again, making me even more confused.

If you have any ideas, please let me know as I'm getting a bit frustrated after being stuck on this for a few days!

candidates.title: [Bug] revert_checkpoint_conversion_mapping crashes with re.error "invalid group reference" on transformers-5.x models
candidates.body:
### Problem Description

Exporting a quantized model whose HF class defines a `checkpoint_conversion_mapping` (transformers 5.x) via `format="llm_compressor"` raises `re.error: invalid group reference 1` inside `revert_checkpoint_conversion_mapping`.

The function strips regex **capture groups** from the *source* pattern (`re.sub(r"\(.*\)", "", source_pattern)`) but leaves the corresponding **backreferences** (e.g. `\1`) in the *target* pattern. `re.subn(source, target, name)` then fails to compile the replacement template because the referenced group no longer exists.

### Reproduction Steps

```python
from auto_round import AutoRound
ar = AutoRound(model="<any Qwen3.5-MoE checkpoint>", scheme="W4A16")
ar.quantize_and_save(output_dir="out", format="llm_compressor")
```

Qwen3.5/3.6-MoE's transformers conversion mapping is e.g.
`{'^model\.language_model\.(.+)$': 'model.\\1', ...}` — the `(.+)` group is stripped from the source while `\1` remains in the target, triggering the error.

### Environment Information

- auto-round 0.14.1
- transformers 5.10.4
- torch 2.12.0+xpu
- Python 3.12.3

### Error Logs

```
File ".../auto_round/utils/common.py", line 1195, in revert_checkpoint_conversion_mapping
    name, n_replace = re.subn(source_pattern, target_pattern, name)
File ".../re/__init__.py", line 334, in _compile_template
    return _sre.template(pattern, _parser.parse_template(repl, pattern))
re.error: invalid group reference 1 at position 22
```

### Additional Context

- The function is imported into multiple modules (`compressors/base.py`, `compressors/shard_writer.py`). The `shard_writer` path only fires when a `layer_config` excludes some layers (mixed-precision quant), so a **uniform** quant can pass while a **mixed** one fails — worth patching in both call sites' shared helper.
- Suggested fix: keep source/target consistent — either do **not** strip the capture group from the source, or strip the backreference from the target whenever the group is stripped from the source.
- Worked around locally by monkeypatching the function to try the intact pattern first and fall back to stripping both sides.

Script

import sys
import argparse
from auto_round import AutoRound

'''

python convert_model_to_fp8.py --input PATH/to/model --out_file PATH/to/output

parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description='Convert a hf model to a hf fp8 static quantized model')
parser.add_argument('--input', type=str, help="directory containing model file")
parser.add_argument('--out_file', type=str, help='path to write to')
args = parser.parse_args()

model_path = args.input
save_path = args.out_file


layer_config = {}

    model=model_path,
    bits=8,

candidates.title: [Feature]: add --dry-run estimation mode
candidates.body:
### Feature Description

Add a `--dry-run` flag to the CLI that estimates VRAM usage, output file size, and approximate quantization time without running the full quantization process. It loads the model config via `AutoConfig.from_pretrained()` (no weights) and prints a summary table, then exits.

### Motivation and Use Case

Users quantizing large models (70B+) need to know resource requirements before committing GPU hours. Currently the only way to find out is to start the process and watch it fail or succeed. A lightweight estimation step would save significant time and compute costs.

This is related to #1551 (reducing quant cost) and #1584 (VRAM tracking) - both involve understanding resource requirements for quantization.

### Alternatives Considered

- Manually calculating estimates from model card metadata - error-prone and tedious
- Running the full process with a tiny calibration set - still loads model weights and takes significant time/memory

### Definition of Done

- [x] `--dry-run` CLI flag prints VRAM, output size, and time estimates
- [x] Python API supports `dry_run=True` parameter in `AutoRound`
- [x] Works for common quantization schemes (W4A16, W2A16, W3A16, W8A16, MXFP4, etc.)
- [x] Unit tests for estimation functions
- [x] Exits cleanly without loading model weights

### Additional Context

The estimation approach:
- Peak VRAM: calculated from parameter count, dtype size, calibration batch size, and sequence length
- Output size: calculated from target bit width and parameter count
- Time: rough estimate from layer count, iterations, and calibration sample count

Estimation uses `AutoConfig.from_pretrained()` to load only the model architecture metadata.

candidates.title: Production report: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B int4-mixed replaced a 4.75-bit build on DGX Spark (GB10), +12.7% decode, no quality loss, vision intact
candidates.body:
Not a bug. This is a production field report; your org settings block discussion creation for OAuth apps, so filing it here. Feel free to convert to a discussion.

Setup: DGX Spark (GB10, 128 GB unified memory), vLLM, `Intel/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-int4-mixed-AutoRound` served with `--quantization gptq`, speculative decoding via a DFlash draft (k=3).

Measured against the 4.75-bit compressed-tensors community build of the same model, same box, same measurement method (prefill-separated 256-token decode, temperature 0, median of 3):

- Decode: 69.2 vs 61.4 tok/s (+12.7%, in line with the bandwidth math for 4.0 vs 4.75 bits on a 273 GB/s bus)
- Quality: 18/18 on a deterministic coding gate (multi-file renames incl. an ambiguous-symbol case, plus structured chat checks; script-graded, no LLM judging). Identical pass rate to the 4.75-bit build.
- The int4-mixed build kept the full vision tower; it reads screenshots correctly once `--language-model-only` is dropped. Of the three quants we compared (AutoRound int4-mixed, 4.75-bit compressed-tensors, FP8) it was the only one with working vision on this box.

It has been the production model here since 2026-06-11. The mixed approach (MoE gate projections at 16-bit) seems to be doing exactly what it promises at this size.

Method details and raw numbers: https://sovgrid.org/blog/qwen3-35b-quant-comparison-autoround-prismaquant-fp8/

candidates.title: AutoScheme not supported in MLLM/VLM mode (Qwen3-VL) — timeline for support?
candidates.body:
**Description:**

I’m trying to use **AutoScheme** (adaptive mixed-bit scheme search) with a **multimodal (VLM/MLLM)** model, but AutoRound currently reports that AutoScheme is not supported for multimodal LLMs.

---

## What I’m doing

Model: `Qwen/Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B-Instruct`  
Goal: automatically pick a mixed scheme close to **avg_bits=2.8** using options like `("W2A16", "W4A16")` on real **image+prompt** calibration samples.

Minimal code:

```python
import torch
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader
from transformers import AutoProcessor, Qwen3VLMoeForConditionalGeneration
from auto_round import AutoRound, AutoScheme

model_id = "Qwen/Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B-Instruct"

model = Qwen3VLMoeForConditionalGeneration.from_pretrained(
    model_id,
    torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16,
    device_map={"": 0},
)
model.eval()

processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id)
tokenizer = processor.tokenizer  # pass tokenizer to AutoRound for VLM

# dataset provides (image, prompt) samples, collator builds model inputs
ds = JsonlImagePromptDataset("/path/to/valid.jsonl")
collate = Qwen3VLCollator(processor=processor, image_dir="/path/to/images")

def collate_to_device(batch):
    inputs = collate(batch)
    inputs.pop("token_type_ids", None)
    return inputs.to(model.device)

loader = DataLoader(ds, batch_size=1, shuffle=True, num_workers=0, collate_fn=collate_to_device)

scheme = AutoScheme(
    avg_bits=2.8,
    options=("W2A16", "W4A16"),
    ignore_scale_zp_bits=True,
    batch_size=1,
)

ar = AutoRound(
    model=model,
    tokenizer=tokenizer,
    scheme=scheme,
    dataset=loader,
    nsamples=200,
    seqlen=3000,
    iters=200,
    batch_size=1,
    low_gpu_mem_usage=False,
    device_map=0,
    quant_nontext_module=False,  # I don't want to quantize vision modules
)

ar.quantize_and_save(output_dir="./out", format="auto_round")
```

## What happens

AutoRound detects VLM mode and then prints:

- `INFO ... using MLLM mode for multimodal model.`
- `INFO ... AutoScheme is not yet supported for multimodal LLMs.`

So AutoScheme cannot be used in this setup.

## Expected behavior

I expected AutoScheme to be usable for multimodal models at least in the sense of:
- allowing multimodal (image+prompt) calibration/tuning runs, and selecting mixed W2/W4 schemes for the LLM part based on the actual **multimodal forward path**.


## Why it matters

My use case is **OCR with a VLM** (documents/screenshots). **Visual tokens are crucial** here because the LLM’s reasoning and decoding quality depends on the visual evidence being injected correctly into the language backbone.

Importantly: **I do NOT plan to quantize the visual modules** (vision encoder / projector). I want to keep them in higher precision (that’s why `quant_nontext_module=False`).  
However, even if the vision side is kept unquantized, it still **changes which parts of the LLM are active and how they are used**: the presence of visual tokens affects attention patterns, MLP activations, and in MoE models potentially **expert routing / activation distribution** inside the LLM.

So for OCR workloads, it’s not enough to run AutoScheme on text-only calibration prompts. To pick good mixed-bit allocations (e.g. W2/W4 for `avg_bits=2.8`), AutoScheme needs to work in **multimodal mode**, using **image+prompt** samples, because that is the forward path that determines which LLM weights matter most under visual conditioning.

---

## Questions

Is **AutoScheme support for multimodal (VLM/MLLM) models** on your roadmap?  
If yes, could you share an **estimated timeline / milestone** (or what is blocking it)?

Thanks!

candidates.title: [Bug]: AutoRound 0.13 quantizes MoE router gate and embedding for Intel/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-W4A16-AutoRound
candidates.body:
# [Bug]: AutoRound 0.13 quantizes MoE router gate and embedding for `Intel/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-W4A16-AutoRound` — should be excluded

## Summary

`Intel/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-W4A16-AutoRound` (autoround 0.13.0, model_free WOQ) emits W4A16-quantized weights for two layer classes that should remain in higher precision per standard MoE quantization convention:

1. **The MoE router gate** (`layers.N.ffn.gate.qweight` / `qzeros` / `scales` for all 43 layers, 256 experts each)
2. **The token embedding** (`embed.qweight` / `qzeros` / `scales`)

The model's `quantization_config.json` `extra_config` block only excludes `head` (lm_head):

```json
"extra_config": {
  "head": { "bits": 16, "data_type": "float" }
}
```

## Why this matters

- **Routers in MoE models are tiny and quality-critical.** For DeepSeek-V4-Flash: 256 experts × hidden_size 4096 = ~1 MB per layer × 43 layers = ~43 MB total. Quantizing them saves negligible memory but degrades expert selection accuracy. Every other major MoE quant pipeline I've seen (compressed-tensors, AWQ, GPTQ as practiced by cyankiwi/QuantTrio) keeps the router in FP16/BF16.
- **Embeddings benefit very little from W4 quantization** and lose meaningful accuracy. Same convention: keep them in original precision.
- The model also emits a custom `tid2eid` field per gate layer (`layers.N.ffn.gate.tid2eid`) that downstream loaders (e.g. vLLM's `DeepseekV4ForCausalLM`) don't recognize, suggesting an Intel-specific routing-table extension layered on top of the quantized gate.

## Practical impact

vLLM's canonical `DeepseekV4ForCausalLM.load_weights` expects an unquantized router and embedding. Loading this model produces:

```
KeyError: 'layers.0.ffn.gate.qweight'
   File ".../vllm/model_executor/models/deepseek_v4.py", line 1365, in load_weights
       param = params_dict[name]
```

The model is currently **unloadable in vLLM as-is**. Workarounds (patching vLLM to handle a quantized router) would be unsafe — routing accuracy degrades sharply with W4 weights.

## Suggested fix

Extend the `extra_config` exclusion list in the model's quantization config to keep router and embedding in FP16:

```diff
 "extra_config": {
-  "head": { "bits": 16, "data_type": "float" }
+  "head":           { "bits": 16, "data_type": "float" },
+  "embed":          { "bits": 16, "data_type": "float" },
+  "*.ffn.gate":     { "bits": 16, "data_type": "float" }
 }
```

(Glob pattern syntax assumed — adapt to whatever format auto-round uses. The intent: keep `embed.weight`, `lm_head.weight`, and every layer's `ffn.gate.weight` unquantized.)

For the toolchain itself: it would be reasonable to **default-exclude routers for any MoE-family model** (deepseek_v3/v4, qwen2_moe, qwen3_moe, mixtral, jamba, nemotron_h, etc.) so users don't have to discover this case-by-case. This would slot in alongside the model-specific work in #1711 (Nemotron-H/Cascade-2) and #1689 (Qwen3.5-MoE).

## Reproduction

```python
import json
# Show the quantized router weights
with open('/path/to/Intel--DeepSeek-V4-Flash-W4A16-AutoRound/model.safetensors.index.json') as f:
    idx = json.load(f)
gate_keys = sorted(k for k in idx['weight_map'] if 'gate' in k and 'layers.0' in k)
print(gate_keys)
# Output:
# ['layers.0.ffn.gate.qweight',
#  'layers.0.ffn.gate.qzeros',
#  'layers.0.ffn.gate.scales',
#  'layers.0.ffn.gate.tid2eid']

embed_keys = sorted(k for k in idx['weight_map'] if 'embed' in k.lower())
print(embed_keys)
# Output:
# ['embed.qweight', 'embed.qzeros', 'embed.scales']
```

## Evidence summary

- `quantization_config.json` from the published model: only excludes `head`
- All 43 layers' `ffn.gate.*` are quantized: confirmed via safetensors index
- `embed.*` is quantized: confirmed via safetensors index
- `tid2eid` extension present on every gate layer (Intel-specific)
- Quantization config: `model_free: true, iters: 0` (this is a pure quant pass on top of an existing model — model_free WOQ from #1699)

## Environment

- Model: `Intel/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-W4A16-AutoRound` (HF, current as of 2026-05-03)
- AutoRound version (per quant config): `0.13.0`
- Downstream loader tested: vLLM 0.20.1.dev0 (also reproduces on 0.20.1 GA — vLLM's `DeepseekV4ForCausalLM.load_weights` makes the canonical router-is-FP16 assumption)

## Related

- intel/auto-round #1711, #1712 (Nemotron-H MoE support work)
- intel/auto-round #1689 (Qwen3.5-MoE: similar dry-run / config edge case for MoE)
- intel/auto-round #1699 (`model_free` WOQ — the codepath that produced this artifact)
- vllm-project/vllm: I'm filing a separate vLLM-side issue today for the bare `KeyError: 'scale_fmt'` that surfaces *before* this router-shape mismatch on the same model. (The two are independent — vLLM crashes earlier because of an unrelated hardcoded config lookup; even after that's fixed, the router quantization issue is still fatal.)

— MidasMining, 8× RTX A4000 SM86 / vLLM 0.20.1

candidates.title: [Bug] GGUF Q6_K export writes NaN block scales for all-zero blocks (0/0 in make_qx_quants_chunk) — NaN logits in llama.cpp
candidates.body:
## Summary

The GGUF Q6_K export path writes **NaN block scales** (the fp16 `d` at the end of each 210-byte Q6_K block) for blocks whose source weights are **all zero** — e.g. padded/unused vocab rows in an embedding tensor. A single NaN scale poisons the whole forward pass: the GGUF loads fine, but llama.cpp inference returns NaN logits/PPL for any batch touching those rows.

## Environment

- auto-round **v0.13.0** (also present on current `main` — the affected code is unchanged)
- Observed with the CLI:

```bash
auto-round --model google/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-qat-q4_0-unquantized \
  --format "gguf:q4_0" --iters 200 --nsamples 256 --seqlen 2048
```

## Observed behavior

The exported model's `token_embd.weight` (Q6_K, 2,883,584 blocks) contained **exactly 17 NaN `d` scales**. Every one was on a block whose quantized payload was uniformly zero (verified: payload min=max=0). Affected token rows included 107, 528, 532, 558, and a cluster at 236770–236832 — i.e. unused/padded vocab entries whose embedding rows are all zeros.

Patching the 17 scales to `0.0` in the GGUF fully repairs the model — it then scores normal perplexity. So the expected behavior is clear: **all-zero blocks should get `d = 0.0`** (exact reconstruction).

## Root cause

`make_qx_quants_chunk` in `auto_round/export/export_to_gguf/packing.py` (used for Q6_K scale search via `search_gguf_scale_min_sym`) divides without a zero guard:

https://github.com/intel/auto-round/blob/v0.13.0/auto_round/export/export_to_gguf/packing.py#L195-L197

```python
sumlx = (w * chunk * L).sum(dim=-1)
suml2 = (w * L * L).sum(dim=-1)
scales = sumlx / suml2          # 0/0 = NaN for an all-zero group (w = chunk**2 = 0, L = 0)
```

For an all-zero 16-element group, `w = chunk*chunk = 0` and `L = 0`, so this is `0/0 = NaN`. The NaN then slips through every downstream guard:

1. `quant_tensor_gguf_sym_dq` (`auto_round/data_type/gguf.py:818`): `torch.where(torch.abs(scale) < 1e-30, 0, scale)` — `abs(NaN) < 1e-30` is `False`, so the NaN passes through.
2. `double_quant_tensor_sym_rtn` (`auto_round/data_type/gguf.py:242-246`): `argmax` over the NaN-containing abs picks the NaN → `wmax = NaN` → `d_scale = NaN`.
3. `q6_k_quant_block` writes `d_scale` as the block's fp16 `d`.

The refinement loop inside `make_qx_quants_chunk` never repairs it either, because `replace_id = (suml2_tmp > 0) & ...` is `False` when `suml2_tmp` is NaN.

Notably, the original non-chunked `make_qx_quants` (same file, line 270) already has the correct guard — `scales = sumlx * get_reciprocal(suml2)`, where `get_reciprocal` returns 0 for (near-)zero inputs. The chunked rewrite dropped it. llama.cpp's own `make_qx_quants` likewise guards this case (`if (!amax) { scale = 0; ... }`).

## Minimal reproduction (no model needed)

```python
import torch
from auto_round.data_type.gguf import quant_tensor_gguf_sym_dq

t = torch.zeros(2, 256)        # block 0: all zeros (e.g. an unused vocab row)
t[1] = torch.randn(256)
qdq, scales, _ = quant_tensor_gguf_sym_dq(t, bits=6, scale_dtype=torch.float32)
print(scales["scale"][0].flatten()[:4])   # tensor([nan, nan, nan, nan])
print(scales["d_scale"].flatten())        # tensor([nan, ...])
print(torch.isnan(qdq[0]).any())          # True — qdq weights are NaN too
```

## Fix (verified)

One line in `make_qx_quants_chunk`, matching the existing non-chunked implementation:

```python
scales = sumlx * get_reciprocal(suml2)
```

With this change the reproduction above yields sub-scales `0.0`, `d_scale = 0.0`, and exact all-zero reconstruction. Happy to send a PR.

Two adjacent spots probably deserve the same audit:
- `make_qp_quants` (`packing.py:491`) ends with an unguarded `return sumlx / suml2, L` (imatrix super-block path).
- The NaN-transparent `torch.where(torch.abs(scale) < 1e-30, ...)` in `quant_tensor_gguf_sym_dq` could be hardened with `torch.nan_to_num` as defense in depth.

import re
from collections import Counter
from typing import Optional

import torch
from datasets import load_dataset
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer
from auto_round import AutoRound

MODEL_PATH = "google/gemma-4-31B-it"
OUTPUT_DIR = "./INT8-AutoRound"
DATASET_NAME = "NeelNanda/pile-10k"

FP16_PATTERNS = ("lm_head", "vision_tower",)
INT8_PATTERNS = ("self_attn","mlp")
INT8_PROTECT_FIRST = 0
INT8_PROTECT_LAST = 0
INT4_PATTERNS = ()
INT4_PROTECT_FIRST = 0
INT4_PROTECT_LAST = 0

GROUP_SIZE = 128
SYM = True

MAX_SAMPLES = 512
SEQ_LEN = 2048


def get_layer_idx(module_name: str) -> Optional[int]:
    match = re.search(r"\.layers\.(\d+)\.", module_name)
    return int(match.group(1)) if match else None


def compute_boundary_set(num_layers: int, n_first: int, n_last: int) -> set:
    if n_first <= 0 and n_last <= 0:
        return set()
    head = set(range(min(max(n_first, 0), num_layers)))
    tail = set(range(max(0, num_layers - max(n_last, 0)), num_layers))
    return head | tail


def matches_any(name: str, patterns) -> bool:
    if not patterns:
        return False
    return any(p in name for p in patterns)


def build_layer_config(model: torch.nn.Module) -> dict:
    indices = {get_layer_idx(name) for name, _ in model.named_modules()}
    indices.discard(None)
    num_layers = max(indices) + 1 if indices else 0
    print(f"language_model layer count: {num_layers}")

    int8_boundary = compute_boundary_set(num_layers, INT8_PROTECT_FIRST, INT8_PROTECT_LAST)
    int4_boundary = compute_boundary_set(num_layers, INT4_PROTECT_FIRST, INT4_PROTECT_LAST)
    print(f"INT8 boundary layers (-> FP16): {sorted(int8_boundary)}")
    print(f"INT4 boundary layers (-> INT8): {sorted(int4_boundary)}")

    layer_config = {}
    for name, module in model.named_modules():
        if not isinstance(module, torch.nn.Linear):
            continue

        if matches_any(name, FP16_PATTERNS):
            layer_config[name] = {"bits": 16}
            continue

        if matches_any(name, INT8_PATTERNS):
            idx = get_layer_idx(name)
            if idx is not None and idx in int8_boundary:
                layer_config[name] = {"bits": 16}
            else:
                layer_config[name] = {"bits": 8, "group_size": GROUP_SIZE, "sym": SYM}
            continue

        if matches_any(name, INT4_PATTERNS):
            idx = get_layer_idx(name)
            if idx is not None and idx in int4_boundary:
                layer_config[name] = {"bits": 8, "group_size": GROUP_SIZE, "sym": SYM}
            else:
                layer_config[name] = {"bits": 4, "group_size": GROUP_SIZE, "sym": SYM}
            continue


    return layer_config


def collect_calibration_samples(tokenizer) -> list:
    dataset = load_dataset(DATASET_NAME, split="train")
    samples = []

    for item in dataset:
        tokenized = tokenizer(
            item["text"],
            truncation=True,
            max_length=SEQ_LEN,
            return_tensors="pt",
        )

        if tokenized["input_ids"].shape[-1] >= SEQ_LEN:
            samples.append(tokenized.data)

        if len(samples) >= MAX_SAMPLES:
            break

    return samples


def main():
    tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(MODEL_PATH, trust_remote_code=True)

    model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
        MODEL_PATH,
        torch_dtype="auto",
        device_map="meta",
        trust_remote_code=True,
    )

    layer_config = build_layer_config(model)

    bits_counter = Counter(cfg["bits"] for cfg in layer_config.values())
    print(f"Layer count by bits (in layer_config): {dict(bits_counter)}")

    del model
    torch.cuda.empty_cache()

    tokens_list = collect_calibration_samples(tokenizer)

    print(f"len(tokens_list) = {len(tokens_list)}")
    print(f"first input_ids shape  = {tokens_list[0]['input_ids'].shape}")
    print(f"last  input_ids shape  = {tokens_list[-1]['input_ids'].shape}")
    print(f"first dtype = {tokens_list[0]['input_ids'].dtype}")


    ar = AutoRound(
        model=MODEL_PATH,
        tokenizer=tokenizer,
        scheme="W8A16",
        enable_torch_compile=True,
        group_size=GROUP_SIZE,
        sym=SYM,
        layer_config=layer_config,
        dataset=tokens_list,
        device_map="auto",
        batch_size=8,
        seqlen=SEQ_LEN,
        iters=1000,
        nsamples=MAX_SAMPLES
    )
    ar.quantize_and_save(OUTPUT_DIR, format="auto_round:auto_gptq")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

candidates.title: [Bug]: Qwen3.5-9B with quantized lm_head throws exceptions in vLLM serving
candidates.body:
### Problem Description

When quantizing Qwen/Qwen3.5-9B, the output is LARGER than the original model:
- Quantized shards (model-00001/00002): ~8.5 GB  
- model_extra_tensors.safetensors: ~17 GB  ← larger than the 17.98 GB original
- Total output: ~24.5 GB vs 17.98 GB original

### Reproduction Steps

python quantize_autoround.py --model Qwen/Qwen3.5-9B --group-size 128 --iters 100 --scheme W3A16 --output ./Qwen3.5-9B-AutoRound-W3A16-g128-coding --calib coding --quant-lm-head --torch-compile --low-gpu-mem


### Environment Information

- auto-round version: nightly (latest from GitHub)
- model: Qwen/Qwen3.5-9B (model_type: qwen3_5)
- scheme: W3A16 / W4A16, group_size=128
- format: auto_round
- using CPU (not GPU)


### Additional Context


**Root cause**
Qwen3.5-9B uses a hybrid Gated Delta Network (DeltaNet) architecture:
- 24/32 blocks are DeltaNet (linear_attn) with weight dimensions 
  not divisible by group_size (e.g. 409, 1228)
- These layers fail quantization silently:
  WARNING missing_tensors.py L702: Failed to quantize 
  model.language_model.layers.13.linear_attn.in_proj_a.weight: 
  The size of tensor a (409) must match the size of tensor b (410)
- 774 tensors end up in model_extra_tensors.safetensors at bf16

Since DeltaNet layers make up ~75% of model weight, the unquantized 
extra_tensors file is larger than the quantized transformer layers.

**Related**: Issue #1496 mentions similar dimension issues for AWQ export 
with workaround `ignore_modules=["in_proj_ba"]`


**Expected behavior**
Either:
1. Fail early with a clear error: "Model architecture qwen3_5 with 
   DeltaNet layers is not fully supported by AutoRound. These layers 
   will remain at bf16, resulting in larger output than original."
2. Support DeltaNet layer quantization with proper padding/rounding
3. Add Qwen3.5 to the list of partially-supported models in docs

[quantize_autoround.py](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/26446358/quantize_autoround.py)

### Error Logs

candidates.title: [Bug]: Quantized MXFP model export in llmc format failed with inference
candidates.body:
### Problem Description

Quantized and saved the mxfp4/mxfp8 model in llmc format, quantize pass, but inference with transformers failed. 

### Reproduction Steps

Run with PR, https://github.com/intel/neural-compressor/pull/2441  
export CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=5
bash run_quant.sh --topology=Llama-3.1-8B --dtype=mxfp8 --input_model=/models/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct --output_model=/data3/jenkins/saved_models/Llama-3.1-8B_mxfp8_llmc --export_format=llm_compressor
bash run_quant.sh --topology=Llama-3.1-8B --dtype=mxfp4 --input_model=/models/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct --output_model=/data3/jenkins/saved_models/Llama-3.1-8B_mxfp4_llmc --export_format=llm_compressor

python run_prompt.py --saved_model_path=/data3/jenkins/saved_models/Llama-3.1-8B_mxfp8_llmc
python run_prompt.py --saved_model_path=/data3/jenkins/saved_models/Llama-3.1-8B_mxfp4_llmc

### Environment Information

HW: A100 1 card.   
Main SW list: 
torch                             2.9.0
transformers                      4.57.6
compressed-tensors                0.14.0.1
auto-round    https://github.com/intel/auto-round/commit/de0650e1062312c2d13fe2a6d569d9ccdd6398fe 

### Error Logs

The error occurs here: https://github.com/intel/auto-round/blob/81c8ee4262dd0094d736545deac0af8a393ecfb7/auto_round/compressors/base.py#L2190

The cause is due to a mismatch between the list of devices here:
https://github.com/intel/auto-round/blob/81c8ee4262dd0094d736545deac0af8a393ecfb7/auto_round/compressors/base.py#L2172

candidates.title: [Bug]: AWQ export of Qwen3.5-9B (DeltaNet Hybrid) crashes in vLLM due to non-divisible Output Channels (in_proj_ba)
candidates.body:
### Problem Description

**Description:**
I successfully quantized the new `Qwen3.5-9B` hybrid architecture (which features Gated DeltaNets) using AutoRound. However, when exporting the quantized model to the **AWQ** format and serving it with vLLM, the inference engine immediately crashes upon receiving the first prompt. 

The INC native export format works perfectly, but the AWQ export fails during inference.

**Error Log:**
When the forward pass hits the small internal projection layers of the DeltaNet block, vLLM's AWQ C++ kernel throws the following error:
```text
  File "/usr/local/lib/python3.12/site-packages/vllm/model_executor/models/qwen3_5.py", line 169, in forward
    ba, _ = self.in_proj_ba(hidden_states)
...
  File "/usr/local/lib/python3.12/site-packages/vllm/model_executor/layers/quantization/awq.py", line 275, in apply
    out = ops.awq_gemm(reshaped_x, qweight, scales, qzeros, pack_factor)
...
ValueError: OC is not multiple of Group size
```

**Root Cause Analysis:**
The Qwen3.5-9B architecture contains small data-dependent projection layers (like `in_proj_ba` in the linear attention mechanism) where the Output Channels (OC) are very small (e.g., 32 or 64). 

Because the AWQ kernel strictly requires the `OC` dimension to be perfectly divisible by the quantization `group_size` (usually 128), it triggers a fatal `ValueError` during the `awq_gemm` operation. 

**Expected Behavior:**
AutoRound's AWQ export function should automatically detect linear layers where `OC % group_size != 0` (or specifically target the known small projection layers in hybrid architectures like Qwen3.5's DeltaNets) and automatically fall back to bypassing/ignoring them, leaving them in standard `fp16`/`bf16`. 


**Steps to Reproduce:**
1. Quantize `Qwen3.5-9B` using AutoRound with W4A16.
2. Export the result to AWQ format.
3. Load the AWQ model into vLLM using `--quantization awq`.
4. Send any generation request to the server.

**Temporary Workaround:**
Currently, users have to manually identify and pass `ignore_modules=["in_proj_ba", ...]` to the AutoRound API to prevent these layers from being quantized, or rely strictly on the `INC` format.

Thank you for looking into this!

### Reproduction Steps

1. Run the AutoRound quantization script on the new Qwen3.5-9B (Hybrid Gated DeltaNet) architecture.
2. Set parameters to `W4A16` (or `bits=4, group_size=128`) and export the quantized model to the `AWQ` format.
3. Serve the exported AWQ model using vLLM (`vllm serve /path/to/model --quantization awq --enforce-eager`).
4. Send a prompt to the vLLM server via the `/v1/chat/completions` endpoint.
5. See error: `ValueError: OC is not multiple of Group size` immediately during the forward pass at the `in_proj_ba` layer.


### Environment Information


- OS: Windows 11 (running via WSL2 / Docker)
- Python version: 3.12.12 (inside vLLM Docker container)
- AutoRound version: [latest main branch]
- Hardware: NVIDIA RTX 3090 (24GB VRAM)

- Transformers version: `5.1.0` in vLLM docker image 
- Transformers version: `5.2.0` in while Quantization

candidates.title: [Bug/Question] Qwen3-VL-8B AutoRound W4A16 loads correctly in vLLM but fails AWQ export/conversion
candidates.body:
# AutoRound (W4A16) + Qwen3-VL-8B + vLLM (AWQ) Compatibility Issues

## Problem Description

### System Info

- **Model**: `Vishva007/Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct-W4A16-AutoRound`  
  *(Qwen3-VL-8B quantized with AutoRound W4A16)*
- **Environment**:
  - vLLM `0.13.0` (dev build)
  - Transformers (latest)
  - AutoRound (latest)
- **GPU**: NVIDIA L40

---

### Description

I have successfully quantized **Qwen3-VL-8B** using **AutoRound (W4A16)** and pushed it to the Hugging Face Hub.  
This **base AutoRound model works correctly** when deployed with **vLLM 0.13.0 using default settings** (no explicit `--quantization` flag).

However, I run into **two major issues** when attempting to extend or convert this setup.

---

## Issues

### 1. vLLM Deployment as AWQ Fails

When running the model with:

```bash
--quantization awq
````

or when deploying an explicitly exported **AWQ variant**, vLLM crashes with:

```text
KeyError: 'merger.linear_fc1.weight'
```

#### Observations

* vLLM’s **AWQ loader** expects **unquantized vision-merger layers** under keys like:

  ```text
  merger.linear_fc1.weight
  ```

* AutoRound saves these layers using the **full Hugging Face module path**, e.g.:

  ```text
  model.visual.merger.linear_fc1.weight
  ```

* This key mismatch causes vLLM’s AWQ kernel loader to fail.

---

### 2. Transformers Reload / Conversion Failure

When attempting to reload the AutoRound-quantized model using:

```python
AutoModel.from_pretrained(...)
```

the following happens:

* A large number of **UNEXPECTED keys** appear:

  * `qweight`
  * `qzeros`
  * `scales`
* A large number of **MISSING keys** appear:

  * standard `.weight` tensors

As a result:

* The model **does not map quantized weights correctly**
* Layers are **reinitialized with random weights**
* Any attempt to **re-export (AWQ/GPTQ)** becomes invalid

---

## Questions

1. **Export / Key Compatibility**

   * Is there a recommended way to **export or save an AutoRound-quantized Qwen3-VL model** such that:

     * vLLM’s **strict AWQ loader** accepts the key naming
     * especially for **vision merger layers (`merger.*`)**?

2. **Correct Reload Path**

   * What is the **correct way to reload an AutoRound-quantized VLM** in Python for:

     * inspection
     * conversion (AWQ / GPTQ)
   * without triggering **missing/unexpected key errors** or random reinitialization?

3. **vLLM + AutoRound Compatibility**

   * Are there known or recommended steps to ensure **compatibility between AutoRound’s Qwen3-VL outputs and vLLM’s AWQ kernel expectations**?

---

## Reproduction Steps

The full notebook used for quantization and hub export (AutoRound / AWQ / GPTQ):

🔗 **GitHub**
[https://github.com/vishvaRam/AutoRound-Quantaization/blob/main/auto_round_Qwen_3_VL_8B.ipynb](https://github.com/vishvaRam/AutoRound-Quantaization/blob/main/auto_round_Qwen_3_VL_8B.ipynb)

---

## Environment Information

* **vLLM**: 0.13.0
* **GPU**: NVIDIA L40

---

candidates.title: [Question] How to address the sharp decline in output length
candidates.body:
Hi team,

I'm trying to quantize a heavily fine-tuned Qwen3 4B (for Agent tool-use) with `AutoRound` (W4A16), but I'm getting severe performance degradationl.

The Problem:
FP16 model works great.
W4A16 model fails (1:4 win-rate vs FP16) and output is ~25% shorter (e.g., avg. 120 tokens -> 90 tokens), indicating premature stopping.

My Diagnosis:
The model has systemic activation outliers (e.g., `Max Abs Value > 5000` in several `mlp.down_proj` layers), which are caused by the heavy SFT.
The `Prefill` (Prompt) stage is critical; using "Pure Answer" data to calibrate makes performance even worse.
Crucially, my main fix failed: I tried "selective quantization" (using `quant_config` to set `bits=16` for the Top 4 worst outlier layers). This did not help and performance was still just as bad (1:4 win-rate).

My Questions:

1.  How to address the sharp decline in output length
2. Does this failure (even after skipping layers) prove that W4A16 (`AutoRound`/`AWQ`) is fundamentally unsuited for models with systemic SFT-induced activation outliers?
Thanks!

candidates.title: X86InductorQuantizer + torch.export/aoti_compile_and_package never fuses quantized Linear into onednn::qlinear_pointwise (silent fp32 fallback)
candidates.body:
### Description

## Summary

Quantizing a model with `X86InductorQuantizer` (static PT2E quantization) and then
compiling it via `torch.export.export()` + `torch._inductor.aoti_compile_and_package()`
(the AOTInductor deployment path, as opposed to `torch.compile()`) produces a package
where every Linear/GEMM op still executes in fp32. Weights are stored compactly as
int8, and `quantize_per_tensor`/`dequantize_per_channel`/`dequantize_per_tensor` nodes
are correctly inserted by `convert_pt2e()`, but the weight-prepack fusion that should
convert `dequantize -> linear -> quantize` into a fused `onednn::qlinear_pointwise`
(and lower to a VNNI/AVX-512 int8 GEMM) never fires. Every GEMM in the compiled
`.pt2` package instead dequantizes to fp32, computes with the plain
`CppMicroGemmFP32Vec` template, and requantizes the output afterward -- i.e. pure
quantize/dequantize overhead with **zero** compute benefit, and plausibly a net
slowdown versus skipping quantization entirely.

## What we verified on the real model (53MB conformer-style model, same pipeline)

- `convert_pt2e()` output graph: `59 aten.linear.default`, `34 quantized_decomposed.dequantize_per_channel.default`,
  `34 quantized_decomposed.quantize_per_tensor.default`, `34 quantized_decomposed.dequantize_per_tensor.default`
  -- i.e. 34 of the 59 Linear ops are correctly annotated/quantized at this stage.
- Confirmed `torch._inductor.config.pre_grad_custom_pass is xiq.quant_lift_up` (`QuantLiftUp`
  instance) -- correctly registered via `torchao/quantization/pt2e/quantizer/x86_inductor_quantizer.py`'s
  module-level side effect.
- Manually invoked `QuantLiftUp.__call__` directly on the graph -- zero nodes added/removed/changed
  (expected: it only handles attention-style `Linear -> view/permute -> quantize` chains; not
  the bug, just ruled out as the cause).
- Ran the real `aoti_compile_and_package()` three separate times (once with `EXHAUSTIVE`
  autotune + LTO + `freezing=True`, once with Inductor defaults, once repeated) --
  `torch._dynamo.utils.counters["inductor"]` never contains any `qlinear`/`qconv`-related
  key after any of them.
- Directly inspected the generated `*.kernel.cpp` in all three compiled packages: every
  `_micro_gemm_kernel` function takes `const float* A, const float* B, float* C`
  (0 out of 14 signatures use `int8_t*`/`uint8_t*`), and `grep -c onednn` on the generated
  `.cpp` files returns 0.
- `.wrapper.so` is ~44MB vs. ~53MB of fp32 params -- weights are somewhat more compact
  (consistent with int8 storage) but nowhere near the ~4x reduction genuine int8 packing
  would give, and irrelevant anyway since compute happens in fp32 regardless.

## Expected behavior

`dequantize_per_channel(weight) + dequantize_per_tensor(activation) + aten.linear +
quantize_per_tensor(output)` should be fused into `torch.ops.onednn.qlinear_pointwise`
and lowered to an accelerated AVX-512 VNNI int8 GEMM (`CppMicroGemmAVX512VNNI` in
`torch/_inductor/codegen/cpp_micro_gemm.py`), the same way it apparently does through
the documented `torch.compile()` path.

## Actual behavior

Silent fallback: the compiled package is numerically correct but computes every
Linear/GEMM in fp32, with quantize/dequantize conversions wrapped around each one for
no benefit. No warning or error is raised anywhere in the pipeline.

## Questions for maintainers

1. Is `torch.export()` + `aoti_compile_and_package()` an officially supported path for
   PT2E-quantized CPU models at all, or is `torch.compile()` currently the only
   supported route to get real int8 acceleration?
2. If it's meant to work: what's missing from the pipeline above to get the
   weight-prepack fusion (`_register_qlinear_weight_prepack`) to actually match?
3. If it's *not* meant to work yet: could `convert_pt2e`/`aoti_compile_and_package`
   at least emit a warning when quantize/dequantize nodes survive all the way into
   the compiled artifact unfused, rather than silently shipping a package that's
   doing pure quantization overhead with no compute benefit? This seems like an easy
   footgun for anyone following the AOTInductor deployment tutorials with a quantized
   model.

### Steps to reproduce

```python
Expected (if fusion works): "onednn references" > 0, and at least one
_micro_gemm_kernel with int8_t*/uint8_t* args.

Actual (observed bug): onednn references == 0, all _micro_gemm_kernel
signatures use float* -- i.e. weights are quantized to int8 in storage,
but every GEMM still dequantizes to fp32, computes in fp32, then requantizes
the output. Pure quantize/dequantize overhead, zero compute benefit.


import os
import zipfile

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
from torch.export import Dim, export
from torchao.quantization.pt2e.quantize_pt2e import convert_pt2e, prepare_pt2e
import torchao.quantization.pt2e.quantizer.x86_inductor_quantizer as xiq
from torchao.quantization.pt2e.quantizer.x86_inductor_quantizer import X86InductorQuantizer


class MiniConformerLike(nn.Module):
    """Mimics the structural shape of the real model that triggers this:
    a self-attention block (nn.MultiheadAttention) feeding a plain Linear FFN,
    both under the same 2D/3D reshape-heavy pattern PT2E quantization targets.
    """

    def __init__(self, d_model=256, nhead=4, dim_ff=768):
        super().__init__()
        self.attn = nn.MultiheadAttention(d_model, nhead, batch_first=True)
        self.ff1 = nn.Linear(d_model, dim_ff)
        self.ff2 = nn.Linear(dim_ff, d_model)
        self.act = nn.ReLU()

    def forward(self, x):
        attn_out, _ = self.attn(x, x, x, need_weights=False)
        x = x + attn_out
        x = x + self.ff2(self.act(self.ff1(x)))
        return x


def main():
    torch.manual_seed(0)
    model = MiniConformerLike().eval()

    example_inputs = (torch.randn(1, 128, 256),)
    seq_len = Dim("seq_len", min=16, max=512)
    dynamic_shapes = {"x": {1: seq_len}}

    with torch.no_grad():
        ep = export(model, example_inputs, dynamic_shapes=dynamic_shapes)

    quantizer = X86InductorQuantizer()
    quantizer.set_global(xiq.get_default_x86_inductor_quantization_config())
    prepared = prepare_pt2e(ep.module(), quantizer)

    with torch.no_grad():
        prepared(*example_inputs)  # calibrate

    quantized = convert_pt2e(prepared)

    with torch.no_grad():
        quantized_ep = export(quantized, example_inputs, dynamic_shapes=dynamic_shapes)

    import torch._inductor.config as inductor_config
    inductor_config.cpp_wrapper = True
    inductor_config.freezing = True

    package_path = "/tmp/repro_qlinear_fusion_bug.pt2"
    torch._inductor.aoti_compile_and_package(
        quantized_ep,
        package_path=package_path,
    )

    unzip_dir = "/tmp/repro_qlinear_fusion_bug_unzip"
    with zipfile.ZipFile(package_path) as zf:
        zf.extractall(unzip_dir)

    onednn_refs = 0
    float_gemm_kernels = 0
    int8_gemm_kernels = 0
    for root, _dirs, files in os.walk(unzip_dir):
        for f in files:
            if not f.endswith(".cpp"):
                continue
            text = open(os.path.join(root, f), errors="replace").read()
            onednn_refs += text.count("onednn")
            for line in text.splitlines():
                if "_micro_gemm_kernel(" in line and "inline void" in line:
                    pass  # signature spans multiple lines; checked via arg scan below
            # crude scan: look at declared arg types following each micro_gemm_kernel def
            idx = 0
            while True:
                idx = text.find("_micro_gemm_kernel(", idx)
                if idx == -1:
                    break
                snippet = text[idx: idx + 300]
                if "const float*" in snippet:
                    float_gemm_kernels += 1
                if "const int8_t*" in snippet or "const uint8_t*" in snippet:
                    int8_gemm_kernels += 1
                idx += 1

    print(f"onednn references:        {onednn_refs}")
    print(f"float32 micro_gemm kernels: {float_gemm_kernels}")
    print(f"int8/uint8 micro_gemm kernels: {int8_gemm_kernels}")

    if onednn_refs == 0 and float_gemm_kernels > 0 and int8_gemm_kernels == 0:
        print("\nBUG REPRODUCED: quantized Linear layers compiled to fp32 GEMM, "
              "no oneDNN/VNNI fusion.")
    else:
        print("\nDid NOT reproduce with this minimal model -- fusion may be "
              "specific to a different structural pattern. Do not use this "
              "script as-is in the bug report if this happens; investigate "
              "further before filing.")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

candidates.title: ConvRot — Group-wise Regular Hadamard Rotation for W4A4/W8A8 Diffusion Transformer Quantization
candidates.body:
## Description

I'd like to propose adding ConvRot support to torchao — a group-wise rotation-based quantization method that enables plug-and-play W4A4 inference for Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) without retraining.

**Paper**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.03673
**Original implementation** (runs with [torchao](https://github.com/pytorch/ao) on an NVFP4-capable GPU): https://github.com/feice-huang/ConvRot
**My implementation**: https://github.com/gaurav-redhat/ConvRot

## Problem

Current rotation-based quantization in torchao (SpinQuant) uses Sylvester-type Hadamard matrices and targets LLMs. This fails for Diffusion Transformers because:

1. **Row-wise outliers** in DiT activations (e.g., FLUX.1 `proj_out` layers) get amplified by Sylvester's all-ones column — outlier amplitude goes from 14.48 → 106.19
2. **Global rotation** has O(K²) complexity, expensive for large DiT models (12B+ params)
3. **AdaLN design** in DiTs breaks the fusion strategies that make QuaRot fast for LLMs

## Solution: ConvRot

| Feature | SpinQuant (existing) | ConvRot (proposed) |
|---------|---------------------|-------------------|
| Matrix type | Sylvester Hadamard | Regular Hadamard |
| Column discrepancy | n (worst case) | √n (optimal) |
| Scope | Global | Group-wise (N₀=256) |
| Complexity | O(K²) or O(K log K) via FWHT | O(K) |
| Target | LLMs | Diffusion Transformers |
| Row-wise outlier handling | Amplifies | Suppresses (16x better) |
| Implementation | FWHT butterfly ops | Matmul (uses Tensor Cores) |

## Results

Evaluated on SDXL (NVIDIA H200):

| Precision | PSNR↑ | SSIM↑ | LPIPS↓ | Memory Reduction |
|-----------|-------|-------|--------|-----------------|
| BF16 (ref) | — | — | — | 1x |
| **W8A8** | **28.86** | **0.964** | **0.062** | 1.76x |
| **W4A4 mixed** | **18.99** | **0.799** | **0.292** | 1.75x |

Algorithm correctness verified with 66 unit tests (CPU-only, no GPU required):
- Regular Hadamard matrices: orthogonality, regularity confirmed for all orders 4^k
- Outlier suppression: 42–51% reduction in activation max
- Linear equivalence preserved: error < 2.5e-05

## Proposed API

```python
from torchao.prototype.convrot import ConvRotConfig
from torchao.quantization import quantize_

# W8A8 for DiT models
quantize_(model, ConvRotConfig(precision="w8a8", group_size=256))

# W4A4 with mixed precision (sensitive layers stay W8A8)
quantize_(model, ConvRotConfig(
    precision="w4a4",
    group_size=256,
    mixed_precision_layers=["attn.to_out", "attn.to_v"],
))

candidates.title: ZeroPointDomain (class) vs zero_point_domain (variable) typo
candidates.body:
## Description

In `torchao/quantization/utils.py`, the function `groupwise_affine_quantize_tensor_from_qparams` has a typo on line 447 where the **class** `ZeroPointDomain` is compared instead of the **variable** `zero_point_domain`.

**File:** `torchao/quantization/utils.py`  
**Line:** 447

## Current code

```python
if zero_point_domain == ZeroPointDomain.INT:          # line 443 — correct (variable)
    _quantize_affine = quantize_affine
elif zero_point_domain == ZeroPointDomain.FLOAT:      # line 445 — correct (variable)
    _quantize_affine = _quantize_affine_tinygemm
elif ZeroPointDomain == ZeroPointDomain.NONE:          # line 447 — BUG (class, not variable)
    _quantize_affine = _quantize_affine_no_zero_point
else:
    raise ValueError(f"Unrecognized zero point domain: {zero_point_domain}")
```

`ZeroPointDomain` (uppercase) is the **enum class itself**, not the function parameter `zero_point_domain` (lowercase). Comparing an enum class to one of its members is always `False`, so this branch is unreachable.

## Impact

**Medium-High.** Calling `groupwise_affine_quantize_tensor_from_qparams()` with `zero_point_domain=ZeroPointDomain.NONE` always raises `ValueError: Unrecognized zero point domain: ZeroPointDomain.NONE` instead of correctly using `_quantize_affine_no_zero_point`.

## Steps to reproduce

```python
from torchao.quantization.quant_primitives import ZeroPointDomain

# The buggy comparison
zero_point_domain = ZeroPointDomain.NONE

print(zero_point_domain == ZeroPointDomain.NONE)   # True  (correct — variable)
print(ZeroPointDomain == ZeroPointDomain.NONE)      # False (bug — class vs member)
```

## Fix

```diff
- elif ZeroPointDomain == ZeroPointDomain.NONE:
+ elif zero_point_domain == ZeroPointDomain.NONE:
```

## Environment

- **torchao version:** main branch (latest)
- **Python/PyTorch:** Any version (pure Python logic error)
- **OS/Hardware:** Any (platform-independent)


cc @andrewor14 @jerryzh168

I'm happy to submit a PR for this fix if needed.

candidates.title: test_per_row_with_float32: fp32 precision flag leak (tf32) fails tearDown on 1xH100

labels.name: ci-failure
labels.description: Automated report of CI failure on main

candidates.body:
Commits affected: `b862b6edd995ed20bacfec2cc3601c90503179f3`
Run: https://github.com/pytorch/ao/actions/runs/30019749094

## Summary
`quantize_()` unconditionally calls `torch.set_float32_matmul_precision("high")` (via `recommended_inductor_config_setter`), leaking the global fp32-precision flags to `tf32`; PyTorch's new `tearDown` invariant check now flags this and fails `test_per_row_with_float32`.

## Failure details
- Failed job(s): `test (H100, mt-l-x86iamx-22-225-h100, --pre torch torchvision torchaudio ...) / linux-job` (Run 1xH100 Tests)
- Only 1 of 29 tests failed: `1 failed, 28 passed`.
- Representative error (in `torch/testing/_internal/common_utils.py` `tearDown`, not in the test body):
  ```
  FAILED test/dtypes/test_affine_quantized_float.py::TestAffineQuantizedFloat8Compile::test_per_row_with_float32
    - AssertionError: fp32 precision flag leak detected:
        torch.backends.cuda.matmul.fp32_precision: was 'none', became 'tf32'
        torch.backends.mkldnn.matmul.fp32_precision: was 'none', became 'tf32'
  ```

## Root cause
`test_per_row_with_float32` (test/dtypes/test_affine_quantized_float.py:87) calls:
```python
quantize_(model, Float8DynamicActivationFloat8WeightConfig(granularity=PerRow()))
```
on a `float32` model, expecting `AssertionError("PerRow quantization only works for bfloat16 precision")`.

Before that expected assertion fires, the transform handler `_float8_dynamic_activation_float8_weight_transform` (torchao/quantization/quant_api.py:1296) runs — because `set_inductor_config` defaults to `True` — `recommended_inductor_config_setter()`. That helper (torchao/quantization/utils.py:690) calls `torch.set_float32_matmul_precision("high")`, which sets the six global fp32-precision backend flags to `tf32` and never restores them.

The test assertion itself still succeeds (the test body passes). The failure occurs afterward in PyTorch's `TestCase.tearDown`, which recently added a leak check comparing a per-test snapshot of the fp32-precision flags against their post-test values. Because the flags were mutated globally and not restored, the check raises and the test is marked failed.

This is a pre-existing latent flag leak surfaced by the newer PyTorch nightly (`--pre torch`) that introduced the leak check. Note: the triggering commit `b862b6e` only added `.github/` workflow files and did not touch any test or torchao source, so it did not cause this failure — it is reproducible against current `main` on the torch nightly.

## Classification
real regression — the failure is deterministic (1 failed / 28 passed, reproducible), not order- or timing-dependent, so not flaky. It is a genuine test/code interaction (a leaked global mutated by `quantize_`), not an infrastructure problem; the runner log itself notes "This is a script/workflow error, not an infrastructure issue."

## Suggested fix
Any one of the following:

1. Restore the fp32-precision flags around the mutation so `quantize_` does not leak global state. Snapshot and restore in `recommended_inductor_config_setter`, or avoid calling `set_float32_matmul_precision` when it is not needed for the code path.

2. Prevent the config-setter from running in this negative test. Since the test only asserts a validation error, pass `set_inductor_config=False`:
   ```python
   Float8DynamicActivationFloat8WeightConfig(granularity=PerRow(), set_inductor_config=False)
   ```
   Better yet, validate the PerRow/bfloat16 precondition *before* calling `recommended_inductor_config_setter()` in `_float8_dynamic_activation_float8_weight_transform`, so a rejected config never mutates global state.

3. As a stopgap to unblock CI, wrap the mutation/restoration in the test with PyTorch's `recover_orig_fp32_precision` helper, or set `PYTORCH_DISABLE_FP32_PRECISION_LEAK_CHECK=1` (the escape hatch named in the check) — though the intent per the check's docstring is "zero callers", so the real fix is option 1/2.

The cleanest long-term fix is (2)-validate-first combined with (1)-restore, so no `quantize_` call path leaks the global fp32-precision flags.

candidates.title: Blockwise FP8 training GEMMs read past the end of both scale tensors
candidates.body:
### Description

Both Triton GEMMs in `torchao/prototype/blockwise_fp8_training/kernels.py` load their scale tensors without a bounds mask, while every other load and the final store in those kernels is masked. When the autotuner's tile does not divide `M` or `N`, the scale loads dereference memory past the end of `a_s` / `b_s`.

| kernel | unmasked loads |
| --- | --- |
| `triton_fp8_gemm_1x128_128x128_kernel` | `kernels.py:250-251` |
| `triton_fp8_gemm_1x128_128x1_kernel` | `kernels.py:368-369` |

The GEMM output is correct — the out-of-range lanes are dropped by `c_mask` at the store — so this is a memory-safety bug, not a numerical one. It is usually hidden by slack in the caching allocator's slabs, and surfaces as an intermittent `CUDA error: unspecified launch failure` when a scale tensor sits at the tail of a mapped region.

Present on `main` at `03ca489d`.

In the code below, it passes when run normally — which is the problem:

```
$ python repro.py
ok, no NaNs: True
```

Under the sanitizer it faults. `PYTORCH_NO_CUDA_MEMORY_CACHING=1` gives each scale tensor its own `cudaMalloc`, so the stray read is not absorbed by slack after the tensor:

```
$ PYTORCH_NO_CUDA_MEMORY_CACHING=1 compute-sanitizer --tool memcheck python repro.py
========= Invalid __global__ read of size 4 bytes
=========     at triton_fp8_gemm_1x128_128x128_kernel+0xfa0 in kernels.py:251
=========     by thread (64,0,0) in block (0,0,0)
=========     Access to 0x7fa99a418204 is out of bounds
=========     and is 1 bytes after the nearest allocation at 0x7fa99a418200 of size 4 bytes
=========         Host Frame: triton_fp8_gemm_1x128_128x128 in kernels.py:291
========= ERROR SUMMARY: 68 errors
```

### Steps to reproduce

```python
# repro.py
import torch

from torchao.prototype.blockwise_fp8_training.kernels import (
    triton_fp8_blockwise_act_quant_lhs,
    triton_fp8_blockwise_weight_quant_transposed_rhs,
    triton_fp8_gemm_1x128_128x128,
)

M = N = K = 128

A = torch.randn(M, K, dtype=torch.bfloat16, device="cuda")
B = torch.randn(N, K, dtype=torch.bfloat16, device="cuda")

A_q, A_s = triton_fp8_blockwise_act_quant_lhs(A)
B_t_q, B_t_s = triton_fp8_blockwise_weight_quant_transposed_rhs(B)

C = triton_fp8_gemm_1x128_128x128(A_q, B_t_q, A_s, B_t_s, out_dtype=torch.bfloat16)
torch.cuda.synchronize()
print("ok, no NaNs:", not C.isnan().any().item())
```

### Environment

```text
- NVIDIA B200 (SM100)
- torch 2.13.0+cu130, triton 3.7.1
- `compute-sanitizer` from CUDA 13.1.1
- torchao `main` at `03ca489d`
```

candidates.title: Inverted bias flag in replace_conv2d_1x1 inside swap_conv2d_1x1_to_linear
candidates.body:
## Description

In `swap_conv2d_1x1_to_linear`, the `bias` argument passed to `nn.Linear` is logically inverted — it creates a bias when the original conv has none, and skips it when the conv has one.

**File:** `torchao/quantization/quant_api.py`  
**Line:** 234–238

## Current code

```python
def replace_conv2d_1x1(conv):
    assert conv.kernel_size == (1, 1)
    lin = torch.nn.Linear(
        conv.in_channels, conv.out_channels, bias=(conv.bias is None)  # inverted
    )
    lin.weight = torch.nn.Parameter(conv.weight.squeeze(-1, -2))
    lin.bias = conv.bias
    return PermuteSandwich(lin)
```



## Steps to reproduce
```python
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

# Step 1: Create a Conv2d WITHOUT bias
conv = nn.Conv2d(3, 16, 1, bias=False)

# Step 2: See what the buggy code passes to nn.Linear
print(f"conv.bias is None     = {conv.bias is None}")      # True
print(f"conv.bias is not None = {conv.bias is not None}")   # False

# Step 3: Buggy path — nn.Linear allocates an unnecessary bias
lin_buggy = nn.Linear(3, 16, bias=(conv.bias is None))   # bias=True (WRONG)
print(f"lin_buggy.bias = {lin_buggy.bias is not None}")    # True — wasted allocation

# Step 4: Fixed path — nn.Linear correctly skips bias
lin_fixed = nn.Linear(3, 16, bias=(conv.bias is not None))  # bias=False (CORRECT)
print(f"lin_fixed.bias = {lin_fixed.bias is not None}")     # False — clean

# Step 5: After lin.bias = conv.bias, both end up the same
lin_buggy.bias = conv.bias   # overwrites with None
lin_fixed.bias = conv.bias   # already None

print(f"lin_buggy.bias is None = {lin_buggy.bias is None}")  # True
print(f"lin_fixed.bias is None = {lin_fixed.bias is None}")  # True
```

candidates.title: torchao 0.17.0+xpu: MPS module raises RuntimeError, escaping pkgutil's ImportError handler
candidates.body:
### Description

The `experimental/ops/mps/` module calls `_load_torchao_mps_lib()` eagerly
at import time (`__init__.py` line 3). This function follows different code
paths on CUDA vs XPU, ultimately raising a RuntimeError on XPU.

Technical details:

`mps/utils.py::_load_torchao_mps_lib()` has two guard layers:
  Layer 1: check if `torch.ops.torchao._linear_fp_act_*` operators are registered.
  Layer 2: search for `libtorchao_ops_mps_aten.dylib` (macOS dynamic library).

- CUDA wheel: Layer 1 succeeds (operators are registered) → immediate return.
  Layer 2 is never reached.
- XPU wheel: operators are NOT registered → falls through to Layer 2 →
  `.dylib` does not exist on Windows → raises RuntimeError.

The critical impact: RuntimeError is NOT a subclass of ImportError.
`pkgutil.walk_packages()` (used by diffusers, transformers, and other
libraries for backend discovery) catches only ImportError internally.
The unhandled RuntimeError aborts the entire subpackage enumeration.

Cross-environment verification:
- Direct import of `torchao.experimental` etc.: ✅ OK
- `pkgutil.walk_packages(torchao.__path__)`: 🔴 crashes at `mps`
- After removing the `mps/` directory: ✅ walk_packages completes normally
- CUDA torchao 0.17.0 (same version): ✅ walk_packages completes normally

This is an XPU wheel packaging defect: the MPS Python wrapper module is
shipped in the wheel, but the corresponding `torch.ops.torchao` operators
are not registered, and the macOS `.dylib` file does not exist on Windows.
The CUDA wheel avoids this by successfully returning at Layer 1.

Suggested fix: exclude `torchao/experimental/ops/mps/` from the XPU wheel
build, or make `_load_torchao_mps_lib()` lazy (defer to first actual MPS
API call).


### Steps to reproduce

```python
Environment:
- Windows 11 + Intel Arc A770
- PyTorch 2.13.0+xpu
- torchao 0.17.0+xpu (installed via: pip install torchao --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/xpu)
- oneAPI 2025.3.1

1. Verify basic imports are healthy (rule out global import issues):
   python -c "import torchao; from torchao.experimental import quant_api; print('OK')"
   Expected: "OK"

2. Trigger pkgutil.walk_packages (simulates diffusers backend discovery):
   python -c "import pkgutil,torchao;list(pkgutil.walk_packages(torchao.__path__))"
   Result: RuntimeError: Could not find libtorchao_ops_mps_aten.dylib.

3. Verify targeted importlib imports bypass the issue:
   python -c "import importlib,torchao;[importlib.import_module(m) for m in ['torchao.experimental','torchao.quantization','torchao.dtypes']];print('OK')"
   Expected: "OK"

4. Remove MPS module to confirm it is the sole cause:
   Delete directory: site-packages/torchao/experimental/ops/mps/
   Re-run step 2.
   Expected: walk_packages completes normally.

5. Compare CUDA torchao (same version, pip install torchao==0.17.0):
   Re-run step 2.
   Expected: walk_packages completes normally.
```

### Environment

```text
Environment:
- Windows 11 + Intel Arc A770
- PyTorch 2.13.0+xpu
- torchao 0.17.0+xpu (installed via: pip install torchao --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/xpu)
- oneAPI 2025.3.1
```
