candidates.title: llmcompressor W8A8 is slower than FP16
candidates.body:
I use the [offical script](https://github.com/vllm-project/llm-compressor/tree/main/examples/quantization_w8a8_int8) to generate W8A8 Llama3-8B-Instruct models and write a offline inference to test the inference speed. Surprisingly I found that W8A8 model decoding speed is lower than the FP16 model. here is my script. I run the script on a H20-3e GPU with vllm=0.18.0, llmcompressor==0.9.0.2 and torch==2.10.0

```python
"""
Compare performance between FP16 and W8A8 quantized models

Example usage:
python /home/aocheng/vllm/examples/offline_inference/compare_fp16_vs_w8a8.py \
    --fp16-model /home/shared/models/meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct \
    --w8a8-model /home/shared/models/meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct-W8A8-Dynamic-Per-Token/ \
    --batch-size 1 \
    --prompt-size 256 \
    --max-tokens 128 \
    --num-runs 5 \
    --warmup-runs 3
"""
from __future__ import annotations

import subprocess
import sys
import time
from dataclasses import dataclass

from vllm import LLM, EngineArgs
from vllm.utils.argparse_utils import FlexibleArgumentParser

DEFAULT_FP16_MODEL = "/home/shared/models/meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct"
DEFAULT_W8A8_MODEL = "/home/shared/models/meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct-W8A8-Dynamic-Per-Token/"


@dataclass
class BenchmarkResult:
    model_name: str
    model_type: str  # "FP16" or "W8A8"
    load_time: float
    memory_used_mb: float
    infer_time_mean: float
    infer_time_std: float
    prefill_time_mean: float
    decode_time_mean: float
    ttft_mean: float
    itl_mean: float
    input_throughput_mean: float
    output_throughput_mean: float
    total_throughput_mean: float


def get_gpu_memory_info() -> dict[str, float]:
    """Get GPU memory info in MB."""
    try:
        result = subprocess.run(
            ["nvidia-smi", "--query-gpu=memory.used,memory.total", "--format=csv,noheader,nounits"],
            capture_output=True, text=True, check=True
        )
        lines = result.stdout.strip().split("\n")
        if lines:
            used, total = lines[0].split(",")
            used_mb = float(used.strip())
            total_mb = float(total.strip())
            return {"used": used_mb, "total": total_mb, "free": total_mb - used_mb}
    except Exception:
        pass
    return {"used": 0, "total": 0, "free": 0}


def build_prompt_by_tokens(tokenizer, prefix: str, target_tokens: int) -> str:
    """Build prompt by target token count."""
    if target_tokens <= 0:
        return ""
    if not prefix:
        prefix = " "

    prefix_tokens = tokenizer.encode(prefix, add_special_tokens=False)
    prefix_token_count = len(prefix_tokens)

    if prefix_token_count == 0:
        return ""

    repeat_count = (target_tokens + prefix_token_count - 1) // prefix_token_count
    repeated = prefix * repeat_count

    all_tokens = tokenizer.encode(repeated, add_special_tokens=False)
    if len(all_tokens) > target_tokens:
        all_tokens = all_tokens[:target_tokens]

    return tokenizer.decode(all_tokens)


def run_benchmark(model_path: str, model_type: str, args: dict) -> BenchmarkResult:
    """Run benchmark for a single model."""
    import statistics
    from vllm.v1.metrics.reader import Histogram

    max_tokens = args["max_tokens"]
    batch_size = args["batch_size"]
    prompt_size = args["prompt_size"]
    prompt_prefix = args["prompt_prefix"]
    num_runs = args["num_runs"]
    warmup_runs = args["warmup_runs"]

    # Build engine args
    engine_args = {k: v for k, v in args.items()
                   if k not in ["max_tokens", "batch_size", "prompt_size", "prompt_prefix",
                               "num_runs", "warmup_runs", "fp16_model", "w8a8_model"]}
    engine_args["model"] = model_path

    print(f"\n{'='*60}")
    print(f"Loading model: {model_path} ({model_type})")
    print(f"{'='*60}")

    mem_before = get_gpu_memory_info()

    load_start = time.perf_counter()
    llm = LLM(**engine_args)
    load_end = time.perf_counter()

    mem_after = get_gpu_memory_info()
    memory_used = mem_after["used"] - mem_before["used"]

    print(f"Load time: {load_end - load_start:.3f} s")
    print(f"GPU memory used: {memory_used:.0f} MB ({memory_used/1024:.2f} GB)")

    # 构建 prompt
    sampling_params = llm.get_default_sampling_params()
    sampling_params.max_tokens = max_tokens
    sampling_params.min_tokens = max_tokens
    sampling_params.ignore_eos = True

    tokenizer = llm.get_tokenizer()
    prompt = build_prompt_by_tokens(tokenizer, prompt_prefix, prompt_size)
    prompts = [prompt] * batch_size

    # Warmup
    if warmup_runs > 0:
        print(f"Warmup ({warmup_runs} runs)...")
        for i in range(warmup_runs):
            _ = llm.generate(prompts, sampling_params)

    # Multiple runs
    infer_times = []
    prefill_times = []
    decode_times = []
    ttft_times = []
    itl_times = []
    input_throughputs = []
    output_throughputs = []
    total_throughputs = []

    print(f"Benchmark ({num_runs} runs)...")
    for run_idx in range(num_runs):
        infer_start = time.perf_counter()
        outputs = llm.generate(prompts, sampling_params)
        infer_end = time.perf_counter()

        infer_time = infer_end - infer_start
        infer_times.append(infer_time)

        metrics = llm.get_metrics()
        prefill_time = 0.0
        decode_time = 0.0
        ttft = 0.0
        itl = 0.0

        for metric in metrics:
            if isinstance(metric, Histogram):
                if metric.name == "vllm:request_prefill_time_seconds":
                    prefill_time = metric.sum
                elif metric.name == "vllm:request_decode_time_seconds":
                    decode_time = metric.sum
                elif metric.name == "vllm:time_to_first_token_seconds":
                    ttft = metric.sum
                elif metric.name == "vllm:inter_token_latency_seconds":
                    itl = metric.sum

        prefill_times.append(prefill_time)
        decode_times.append(decode_time)
        ttft_times.append(ttft)
        itl_times.append(itl)

        total_output_tokens = sum(len(o.outputs[0].token_ids) for o in outputs)
        total_input_tokens = sum(len(o.prompt_token_ids) for o in outputs)
        input_throughputs.append(total_input_tokens / infer_time)
        output_throughputs.append(total_output_tokens / infer_time)
        total_throughputs.append((total_input_tokens + total_output_tokens) / infer_time)

        print(f"  Run {run_idx+1}: {infer_time:.3f}s, throughput={total_throughputs[-1]:.2f} tok/s")

    # Calculate statistics
    def stats_mean_std(values):
        if len(values) == 0:
            return 0.0, 0.0
        if len(values) == 1:
            return values[0], 0.0
        return statistics.mean(values), statistics.stdev(values)

    infer_mean, infer_std = stats_mean_std(infer_times)
    prefill_mean, _ = stats_mean_std(prefill_times)
    decode_mean, _ = stats_mean_std(decode_times)
    ttft_mean, _ = stats_mean_std(ttft_times)
    itl_mean, _ = stats_mean_std(itl_times)
    input_thr_mean, _ = stats_mean_std(input_throughputs)
    output_thr_mean, _ = stats_mean_std(output_throughputs)
    total_thr_mean, _ = stats_mean_std(total_throughputs)

    return BenchmarkResult(
        model_name=model_path,
        model_type=model_type,
        load_time=load_end - load_start,
        memory_used_mb=memory_used,
        infer_time_mean=infer_mean,
        infer_time_std=infer_std,
        prefill_time_mean=prefill_mean,
        decode_time_mean=decode_mean,
        ttft_mean=ttft_mean,
        itl_mean=itl_mean,
        input_throughput_mean=input_thr_mean,
        output_throughput_mean=output_thr_mean,
        total_throughput_mean=total_thr_mean,
    )


def print_comparison_table(fp16_result: BenchmarkResult, w8a8_result: BenchmarkResult):
    """Print comparison table."""
    print(f"\n{'='*80}")
    print("Performance Comparison: FP16 vs W8A8")
    print(f"{'='*80}")

    # Table header
    print(f"\n{'Metric':<25} {'FP16':<20} {'W8A8':<20} {'Difference':<15}")
    print("-" * 80)

    # Load time
    diff_load = w8a8_result.load_time - fp16_result.load_time
    diff_load_pct = (diff_load / fp16_result.load_time) * 100 if fp16_result.load_time > 0 else 0
    print(f"{'Load time (s)':<25} {fp16_result.load_time:<20.3f} {w8a8_result.load_time:<20.3f} {diff_load_pct:+.1f}%")

    # Memory usage
    diff_mem = w8a8_result.memory_used_mb - fp16_result.memory_used_mb
    diff_mem_pct = (diff_mem / fp16_result.memory_used_mb) * 100 if fp16_result.memory_used_mb > 0 else 0
    print(f"{'GPU memory (MB)':<25} {fp16_result.memory_used_mb:<20.0f} {w8a8_result.memory_used_mb:<20.0f} {diff_mem_pct:+.1f}%")

    print("-" * 80)

    # Inference time
    diff_infer = w8a8_result.infer_time_mean - fp16_result.infer_time_mean
    diff_infer_pct = (diff_infer / fp16_result.infer_time_mean) * 100 if fp16_result.infer_time_mean > 0 else 0
    print(f"{'Inference time (s)':<25} {fp16_result.infer_time_mean:.3f} +/- {fp16_result.infer_time_std:.3f}"
          f"{'':<5} {w8a8_result.infer_time_mean:.3f} +/- {w8a8_result.infer_time_std:.3f}"
          f"{'':<5} {diff_infer_pct:+.1f}%")

    # Prefill time
    diff_prefill = w8a8_result.prefill_time_mean - fp16_result.prefill_time_mean
    diff_prefill_pct = (diff_prefill / fp16_result.prefill_time_mean) * 100 if fp16_result.prefill_time_mean > 0 else 0
    print(f"{'Prefill time (s)':<25} {fp16_result.prefill_time_mean:<20.3f} {w8a8_result.prefill_time_mean:<20.3f} {diff_prefill_pct:+.1f}%")

    # Decode time
    diff_decode = w8a8_result.decode_time_mean - fp16_result.decode_time_mean
    diff_decode_pct = (diff_decode / fp16_result.decode_time_mean) * 100 if fp16_result.decode_time_mean > 0 else 0
    print(f"{'Decode time (s)':<25} {fp16_result.decode_time_mean:<20.3f} {w8a8_result.decode_time_mean:<20.3f} {diff_decode_pct:+.1f}%")

    # TTFT
    if fp16_result.ttft_mean > 0 and w8a8_result.ttft_mean > 0:
        diff_ttft = w8a8_result.ttft_mean - fp16_result.ttft_mean
        diff_ttft_pct = (diff_ttft / fp16_result.ttft_mean) * 100
        print(f"{'TTFT (s)':<25} {fp16_result.ttft_mean:<20.3f} {w8a8_result.ttft_mean:<20.3f} {diff_ttft_pct:+.1f}%")

    # ITL
    if fp16_result.itl_mean > 0 and w8a8_result.itl_mean > 0:
        diff_itl = w8a8_result.itl_mean - fp16_result.itl_mean
        diff_itl_pct = (diff_itl / fp16_result.itl_mean) * 100
        print(f"{'ITL (s)':<25} {fp16_result.itl_mean:<20.3f} {w8a8_result.itl_mean:<20.3f} {diff_itl_pct:+.1f}%")

    print("-" * 80)

    # Throughput
    diff_input_thr = w8a8_result.input_throughput_mean - fp16_result.input_throughput_mean
    diff_input_thr_pct = (diff_input_thr / fp16_result.input_throughput_mean) * 100 if fp16_result.input_throughput_mean > 0 else 0
    print(f"{'Input throughput (tok/s)':<25} {fp16_result.input_throughput_mean:<20.2f} {w8a8_result.input_throughput_mean:<20.2f} {diff_input_thr_pct:+.1f}%")

    diff_output_thr = w8a8_result.output_throughput_mean - fp16_result.output_throughput_mean
    diff_output_thr_pct = (diff_output_thr / fp16_result.output_throughput_mean) * 100 if fp16_result.output_throughput_mean > 0 else 0
    print(f"{'Output throughput (tok/s)':<25} {fp16_result.output_throughput_mean:<20.2f} {w8a8_result.output_throughput_mean:<20.2f} {diff_output_thr_pct:+.1f}%")

    diff_total_thr = w8a8_result.total_throughput_mean - fp16_result.total_throughput_mean
    diff_total_thr_pct = (diff_total_thr / fp16_result.total_throughput_mean) * 100 if fp16_result.total_throughput_mean > 0 else 0
    print(f"{'Total throughput (tok/s)':<25} {fp16_result.total_throughput_mean:<20.2f} {w8a8_result.total_throughput_mean:<20.2f} {diff_total_thr_pct:+.1f}%")

    print("=" * 80)

    # Summary
    print("\nSummary:")
    if diff_mem_pct < 0:
        print(f"  + W8A8 saves {abs(diff_mem_pct):.1f}% memory")
    else:
        print(f"  - W8A8 uses {diff_mem_pct:.1f}% more memory")

    if diff_infer_pct < 0:
        print(f"  + W8A8 inference is {abs(diff_infer_pct):.1f}% faster")
    else:
        print(f"  - W8A8 inference is {diff_infer_pct:.1f}% slower")

    if diff_total_thr_pct > 0:
        print(f"  + W8A8 throughput is {diff_total_thr_pct:.1f}% higher")
    else:
        print(f"  - W8A8 throughput is {abs(diff_total_thr_pct):.1f}% lower")


def create_parser() -> FlexibleArgumentParser:
    parser = FlexibleArgumentParser()
    EngineArgs.add_cli_args(parser)

    model_group = parser.add_argument_group("Model parameters")
    model_group.add_argument("--fp16-model", type=str, default=DEFAULT_FP16_MODEL)
    model_group.add_argument("--w8a8-model", type=str, default=DEFAULT_W8A8_MODEL)

    batch_group = parser.add_argument_group("Batch parameters")
    batch_group.add_argument("--batch-size", type=int, default=1)
    batch_group.add_argument("--prompt-size", type=int, default=128)
    batch_group.add_argument("--prompt-prefix", type=str, default="Hello, my name is")
    batch_group.add_argument("--max-tokens", type=int, default=64)

    benchmark_group = parser.add_argument_group("Benchmark parameters")
    benchmark_group.add_argument("--num-runs", type=int, default=3)
    benchmark_group.add_argument("--warmup-runs", type=int, default=1)

    return parser


def main():
    parser = create_parser()
    args = vars(parser.parse_args())

    fp16_model = args.get("fp16_model", DEFAULT_FP16_MODEL)
    w8a8_model = args.get("w8a8_model", DEFAULT_W8A8_MODEL)

    print(f"\n{'='*80}")
    print("FP16 vs W8A8 Quantized Model Performance Comparison")
    print(f"{'='*80}")
    print(f"FP16 model: {fp16_model}")
    print(f"W8A8 model: {w8a8_model}")
    print(f"Batch size: {args['batch_size']}")
    print(f"Prompt size: {args['prompt_size']} tokens")
    print(f"Max tokens: {args['max_tokens']}")
    print(f"Runs: {args['num_runs']} (warmup: {args['warmup_runs']})")

    # Run FP16 first
    fp16_result = run_benchmark(fp16_model, "FP16", args)
    del fp16_model
    # Clear GPU memory
    import gc
    import torch
    gc.collect()
    if torch.cuda.is_available():
        torch.cuda.empty_cache()

    # Run W8A8
    w8a8_result = run_benchmark(w8a8_model, "W8A8", args)

    # Print comparison table
    print_comparison_table(fp16_result, w8a8_result)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

labels.description: For any issue / PR related to AWQ support

candidates.body:
# Summary

Similar to SmoothQuant, AWQ determines and applies smoothing scales. This process is facilitated by a set of model specific mappings which indicate the activation layers to smooth. Once smoothing is complete, the modifier applies redundant code that is already present within the QuantizationModifier to determine optimal quantization scales and zero_points

The scope of this task is to simplify this modifier by:

1. Removing all the code responsible for generating the quantization scales and zero-points. AWQ, like SmoothQuant, should have the ability to be used in a stackable manner with other quantization modifiers such as the GPTQModifier and QuantizationModifier. 

Examples 1:

```python

recipe = [
    AWQModifier(...),
    QuantizationModifier(...)
]
```
Examples 2:

```python

recipe = [
    AWQModifier(...),
    GPTQModifier(...)
]
```

Example 3:

```python

recipe = [
    AWQModifier(...),
    QuIPModifier(
        rotations=["v", "u"], transform_block_size=128, transform_type="hadamard"
    ),
    QuantizationModifier(targets="Linear", scheme="W4A16", ignore=["lm_head"]),
]
```

2. Simplify the modifier. This can be done by targeting key functionality that is quite complex, such as `_compute_best_scale`


# Implementation Steps

1. Remove quantization scale and zero-point generation code and ensure AWQ can be used in a stackable manner with other quantization modifiers. Validate this through additional test scripts.
2. Make other simplifications within the modiifer to improve the complexity of the modifier
3. Update all examples and tests using the AWQModifier to now use `AWQModifier` stacked with the `QuantizationModifier`. Validate performance and accuracy remains the same
4. As the AWQModifier will still require quantization arguments to generate the means, potentially add a recipe validation step to validate that these arguments match the quantization arguments passed to the subsequent quantization modifier, such as GPTQModifier and QuantizationModifier

candidates.title: [RFC] [Performance Refactor][Distributed] Sequential Onloading with Data-Parallel Calibration and Weight-Parallel Optimization

type.name: Feature
type.description: A request, idea, or new functionality

candidates.body: # Background In order to reduce GPU memory requirements and enable the compression of large models, LLM Compressor calibrates and optimizes models using layer-wise calibration. This [SequentialPipeline](https://github.com/vllm-project/llm-compressor/blob/main/src/llmcompressor/pipelines/sequential/pipeline.py#L31) is very memory efficient, but is only capable of utilizing one GPU at a time, creating a serious performance bottleneck for large models. # Proposal: Sequential Onloading with Data-Parallel Calibration and Weight-Parallel Optimization This design dramatically increases GPU utilization and reduces runtime while maintaining the same low memory utilization per GPU. The idea is to perform calibration with data parallelism and perform optimization with weight parallelism. For each layer 1. Onload layer 2. (DP) Calibration pass 3. (WP) Weights are optimized 4. Update offloaded weights and broadcast across ranks 5. (DP) Propagation pass ## Multiprocessing and Model Replicas In order to load model replicas across ranks, this design proposes using `torchrun` to start multiple processes, each with its own model replica. As with typical DDP, each process will run instructions in parallel and utilize `torch.distributed` for synchronization operations such as weight updates and broadcasting. ## Data Parallel Calibration and Propagation By using data parallelism during calibration and propagation, LLM Compressor can maximize GPU utilization and throughput. In typical DP, the entire model is replicated across each device. The same principle applies here, but instead of replicating the entire model, we only replicate the layer that is onloaded at the given moment. ### Data Parallelism In order to achieve data parallelism, each rank must be assigned disjoint partitions of the dataset. In order to conserve CPU memory utilization and avoid issues related to data shuffling, we should partition the dataset before processing it. ```python NUM_SAMPLES_PER_RANK = NUM_SAMPLES // dist.get_world_size() PARTITION_START = NUM_SAMPLES_PER_RANK * dist.get_rank() DATASET_SPLIT = f"train_sft[{PARTITION_START}:{PARTITION_START + NUM_SAMPLES_PER_RANK}]" ``` ### Shared CPU Offload In order to avoid duplicating model memory on the CPU, ranks must offload parameters to CPU memory which is shared across ranks. This can be done using `torch.Tensor.share_memory_` . Full implementation details can be seen [here](https://github.com/vllm-project/compressed-tensors/pull/534). ### Shared Disk Offload For models which are too large to fit into CPU memory, a disk offload will be required. Disk offloading does not required shared memory, as files on disk are already shared between devices. Full implementation details can be seen [here](https://github.com/vllm-project/compressed-tensors/pull/535). ## Weight Parallel Compression The second part of the design aims to parallelize work done by optimization algorithms. All algorithms implemented by LLM Compressor can extended to support distributed computing in the following steps: 1. Reduce calibration artifacts across ranks 2. Calculate new weight values using calibration artifacts in parallel 3. Broadcast new weight values across ranks ### QuantizationMixin Any modules which perform activation quantization should use the following update strategy. First, minimum and maximum values are calculated on local ranks with respect to local data subsets. Then, these min/max statistics are reduced across all ranks. The reduce min/max statistics are then used to calculate and update qparams within each rank, for each parameter. While work is technically duplicated across ranks, the workload of calculating qparams is very small, and almost certainly outweighs the cost of an additional distributed reduce of the final parameters. In order to reduce excessive distributed communication, the reduce and qparam update steps should be done in batches, or at the end of sequential layers. ### GPTQ Unlike QuantizationMixin, calculating qparams for GPTQ takes a significant amount of time (~1s per parameter). In order to reduce runtime, we opt to not duplicate work across ranks, instead only reducing to local ranks and paying the cost of broadcasting the final weight results. ### AutoRound The flow of AutoRound is very similar to traditional data-parallel distributed training flows. Just like traditional DDP, gradients are calculated locally, reduced across ranks, and then used by the optimizer to perform backwards propagation on weights. ### AWQ AWQ is similar to AutoRound in that both algorithms perform local forward passes and loss calculations. AWQ has the added complication that activation means must be all reduced before forward/loss calculations can begin. Just like AWQ, the "optimizer" step is very low workload, so it is better to reduce MSE values across ranks and duplicate smoothing in order to avoid the final broadcast step. # Implementation Steps - [x] Replace accelerate’s offloading with distributed-friendly implementations @kylesayrs - [x] Replace existing CPU offloading logic https://github.com/vllm-project/compressed-tensors/pull/529, https://github.com/vllm-project/compressed-tensors/pull/530, https://github.com/vllm-project/llm-compressor/pull/2148 - [x] Implement distributed cpu offloading https://github.com/vllm-project/compressed-tensors/pull/534 - [x] Implement distributed disk offloading https://github.com/vllm-project/compressed-tensors/pull/535 - [x] Implement a user interface for loading distributed/offloaded models https://github.com/vllm-project/compressed-tensors/pull/572 @kylesayrs @HDCharles - [x] Add data parallelism to LC @HDCharles @yiliu30 - [x] Modify or add examples of distributed model compression @HDCharles - [x] Extend modifiers to support weight-parallel optimization - [x] QuantizationModifier (parallelize both weight and activations) @GOavi101 @Etelis - [x] GPTQModifier @HDCharles - [x] AutoRound @yiliu30 - [x] AWQModifier @HDCharles - [x] SmoothquantModifier @dzhengAP - [x] Parallelize other lifecycle steps - [x] Extend module compression to perform parallel onloading + compression + broadcast across ranks @kylesayrs https://github.com/vllm-project/compressed-tensors/pull/624 - [x] Extend QuantizationModifier to calibrate weights at the start of each epoch in order to reduce device movement @GOavi101 - [x] Extend MoE replacement to perform parallel replacement @dichn

def pixel_shuffle(self, x, scale_factor=0.5):
        n, w, h, c = x.size()
        # N, W, H, C --> N, W, H * scale, C // scale
        x = x.view(n, w, int(h * scale_factor), int(c / scale_factor))
        # N, W, H * scale, C // scale --> N, H * scale, W, C // scale
        x = x.permute(0, 2, 1, 3).contiguous()
        # N, H * scale, W, C // scale --> N, H * scale, W * scale, C // (scale ** 2)

### 🐛 Describe the bug Using `AWQModifier` with `kv_cache_scheme` fails. The first observed error is: ```text AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'strategy' ``` from the `duo_scaling` validation in `AWQModifier.on_initialize()`, where attention modules introduced by `kv_cache_scheme` can have `quantization_scheme.weights = None`. While debugging locally, I modified the guard in `AWQModifier.on_initialize()` to skip modules whose `quantization_scheme.weights` is `None`. That avoided the initial `AttributeError`, but the run then failed later during calibration with a `RecursionError`: ```diff - and hasattr(module.quantization_scheme, "weights") + and module.quantization_scheme.weights is not None ``` ```text RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded ``` This appears to happen because AWQ smoothing replay reuses `past_key_values` after it has been replaced with `QuantizedKVCache`, so the same attention module can receive its own `QuantizedKVCache` and recurse. ### 🛠️ Steps to reproduce ```python from datasets import Dataset from llmcompressor import oneshot from llmcompressor.modifiers.awq import AWQModifier from compressed_tensors.quantization import QuantizationArgs, QuantizationType, QuantizationStrategy from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained("Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B", torch_dtype="auto", device_map="cpu") processor = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("/path/to/local/Qwen3-tokenizer-or-model") dataset = Dataset.from_dict({"text": ["Hello world " * 50]}) recipe = [ AWQModifier( targets="Linear", scheme="W4A16", kv_cache_scheme=QuantizationArgs( num_bits=8, type=QuantizationType.FLOAT, strategy=QuantizationStrategy.TENSOR, symmetric=True, dynamic=False, ), ) ] oneshot( model=model, processor=processor, dataset=dataset, recipe=recipe, max_seq_length=64, num_calibration_samples=1, ) ``` Observed traceback: ```text File ".../llmcompressor/modifiers/awq/base.py", line 200, in on_initialize and module.quantization_scheme.weights.strategy AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'strategy' ``` Additional note from local investigation: after changing that guard to skip `weights is None`, the run proceeded further but then failed with: ```text File ".../compressed_tensors/modeling/kvcache.py", line 142, in _hook bound = inspect.signature(cache.forward).bind(*args, **kwargs) RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded ```

ExllamaLinearKernel cannot implement due to: Exllama only supports float16 activations

candidates.title: [RFC] Add iMatrix weighted MSE observer for weight quantization
candidates.body:
# RFC: Add iMatrix weighted MSE observer for weight quantization

## Background

The importance matrix (iMatrix) technique, introduced in [llama.cpp PR #4861](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/4861), uses calibration-time activation statistics to improve low-bit weight quantization. The core idea is to collect `⟨a_i²⟩` ,the mean squared input activation for each logical input channel, and use these as importance weights during quantization parameter selection. Channels that carry more signal get more careful rounding.

This technique is widely used in the GGUF ecosystem but is not currently available in llm-compressor. This RFC adapts the core iMatrix idea, activation-informed weighting of weight reconstruction error, to the existing observer interface.

## Motivation

1. **MSE observer regression ([#2094](https://github.com/vllm-project/llm-compressor/issues/2094)).** `memoryless_mse` currently underperforms `memoryless_minmax` on downstream tasks. Importance weighting closes 92% of the gap on GSM8K Platinum at W4.

2. **Low-bit quantization quality.** At W3, both `memoryless_minmax` and `memoryless_mse` effectively destroy reasoning capability (GSM8K strict-match 0.08 and 0.15 respectively). Importance weighting recovers it to 0.38, still degraded but functional. This is the difference between an unusable model and a usable one.

## Proposal

A new observer `imatrix_mse` in `src/llmcompressor/observers/imatrix.py`. It extends the existing MSE grid search with one change: quantization error is weighted by per-channel importance.
```
err = sum(importance * |Q(w) - w|^p)    # imatrix_mse
err = sum(|Q(w) - w|^p)                 # memoryless_mse
```

When importance is unavailable, the observer falls back to uniform MSE with a warning.

### Scope

**Supported:** `torch.nn.Linear`, weight-only quantization, `CHANNEL` / `GROUP` / `TENSOR_GROUP` strategies.

**Out of scope:** activation quantization, automatic collection inside `oneshot()`, `TENSOR` strategy, non-`Linear` modules.

### Importance data contract

The observer reads `module._imatrix_importance`: a 1D `float` tensor of shape `(in_features,)` representing `E[x²]` per input channel. Importance is collected externally via `register_forward_pre_hook` before calling `oneshot()`. A working collection example will be provided with the PR.

If the contract is not satisfied, the observer falls back to uniform MSE (`strict=False`, default) or raises (`strict=True`).

### Usage
```yaml
QuantizationModifier:
  config_groups:
    group_0:
      targets: ["Linear"]
      weights:
        num_bits: 4
        observer: imatrix_mse
```

### Files changed

- `src/llmcompressor/observers/imatrix.py`, new file
- `src/llmcompressor/observers/__init__.py`, add export

No changes to existing observers, modifiers, pipelines, or serialization.

## Design decisions

**Why grid search instead of the analytical llama.cpp algorithm?** The analytical approach returns a scale directly; the `Observer` interface requires min/max. We tested an analytical observer variant and found it unstable on 7B+ models due to over-aggressive scale shrinkage on channels with concentrated importance. The bounded grid search produces consistent results across model sizes.

**Why an observer, not a modifier?** The technique modifies only how candidate ranges are scored. It composes with existing recipe/config flows without changes to quantizer kernels.

## Results

### GSM8K Platinum (`Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct`, W4A16)

| Observer | strict-match |
|---|---|
| `memoryless_minmax` | 0.7717 |
| `memoryless_mse` | 0.7213 |
| `imatrix_mse` | 0.7676 |

Reference from [#2094](https://github.com/vllm-project/llm-compressor/issues/2094): MinMax = 0.7767, MSE = 0.7171.

### GSM8K Platinum (`Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct`, W3A16)

| Observer | strict-match |
|---|---|
| `memoryless_minmax` | 0.0786 |
| `memoryless_mse` | 0.1522 |
| `imatrix_mse` | 0.3838 |

At W3, `imatrix_mse` is 5x better than `memoryless_minmax` and 2.5x better than `memoryless_mse`.

### Perplexity, WikiText-2

**W4A16 (`Llama-3.1-8B`):**

| Method | PPL |
|---|---|
| RTN (`memoryless_mse`) | 7.06 |
| `imatrix_mse` | 6.86 (-2.8%) |
| GPTQ | 6.66 (-5.7%) |

**W3A16 (`Llama-3.1-8B`):**

| Method | PPL |
|---|---|
| RTN (`memoryless_mse`) | 15.09 |
| `imatrix_mse` | 10.09 (-33.1%) |

Also validated on `Qwen2.5-7B` with consistent gains (W4 -1.9%, W3 -6.8%).

### Cost

| | RTN | iMatrix | GPTQ |
|---|---|---|---|
| Calibration | None | ~10 min forward pass | Forward pass + Hessian |
| Quantization | ~40s | ~40s | ~800s |
| Memory overhead | 0 | ~5 MB | O(n²) per layer |

## Limitations

- Requires externally populated importance statistics
- Limited to `Linear` modules with clear input-channel mapping
- Does not automate importance collection inside the pipeline
- Benefits depend on importance/layout alignment; uniform activation distributions may see smaller gains

## Future work

- Helper or lightweight modifier for automated importance collection
- Outlier channel detection and protection, preliminary analysis shows top 1% of channels carry ~30-50% of total importance, suggesting significant potential for selective high-precision treatment
- Per-bitwidth hyperparameter tuning, early sweeps indicate that optimal `norm` and `maxshrink` values differ between W3 and W4 regimes, with W3 benefiting from more targeted settings

## Testing

Unit and integration tests following the patterns in [#2110](https://github.com/vllm-project/llm-compressor/pull/2110).

## References

- [llama.cpp PR #4861](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/4861), original iMatrix technique
- [#2094](https://github.com/vllm-project/llm-compressor/issues/2094), MSE observer regression
- [#2110](https://github.com/vllm-project/llm-compressor/pull/2110), MSE vs MinMax observer tests

The llmcompressor community doesn't provide dynamic FP8 per tensor quantization method. I added the following quantization scheme in the quant_scheme.py file of the compressor_tensors library:
```
FP8_TENSOR = dict(
    weights=QuantizationArgs(
        num_bits=8,
        type=QuantizationType.FLOAT,
        strategy=QuantizationStrategy.TENSOR,
        symmetric=True,
        dynamic=False,
    ),
    input_activations=QuantizationArgs(
        num_bits=8,
        type=QuantizationType.FLOAT,
        strategy=QuantizationStrategy.TOKEN,
        symmetric=True,
        dynamic=True,
        observer=None,
    ),
)
```
Using this quantization scheme, I was able to quantize the Qwen3 MOE model, but it failed during inference on vLLM. The key error message is as follows:
```
quant_config.per_out_ch_quant == (quant_config.w1_scale.size(1) == w1_q.size(1))
IndexError: Dimension out of range (expected to be in range of [-1, 0], but got 1)
```
My questions are:
1. Is the quantization scheme I added for dynamic FP8 per tensor quantization correct?
2. Why can't the quantized MOE model run inference on the vLLM framework?

candidates.title: [Compressed Linear] Remove CompressedLinear

labels.name: good follow-up issue
labels.description: A good issue for users with some familiarity of the codebase

labels.name: Refactor
labels.description: Code cleanup and/or improvements to existing features

candidates.body:
## Background ##
`CompressedLinear` is a class used by Compressed Tensors to wrap around `Linear` modules have been compressed (quantized). The `CompressedLinear` class implements a forward function which decompresses the module such that inference can be performed in full precision (but with the same deterministic output as if the layer was compressed).

## Purpose ##
`CompressedLinear` allows users to run evaluation with quantized models using tools such as `lm-eval`. However, this inference is only enabled through decompression, not quantized kernels. In order to reduce lifecycle complexity and clarify the behavior of Compressed Tensors models when running outside of vLLM, we should remove the `CompressedLinear` class. This class can be added back if CT adopts quantized kernels.

## Suggested Steps
- [ ] Remove all code referencing `CompressedLinear` ([entrypoint](https://github.com/vllm-project/compressed-tensors/blob/main/src/compressed_tensors/quantization/lifecycle/apply.py#L157-L170))

- [ ] Add an error message asking users to call `model.dequantize()` before trying to inference a compressed model [here](https://github.com/vllm-project/compressed-tensors/blob/main/src/compressed_tensors/quantization/lifecycle/forward.py#L373C9-L373C19). This error message should theoretically never occur due to the next steps.

- [ ] At the end of `apply_quantization_config`, check if the model is an instance of `PreTrainedModel` [here](https://github.com/vllm-project/compressed-tensors/blob/116ce4c219df79695391999649b6128bde63e458/src/compressed_tensors/quantization/lifecycle/apply.py#L184). If it is, add a wrapper around `model.post_init`. This wrapper should call `ModelCompressor.from_pretrained_model(model).decompress_model(model)`.

- [ ] The method of dequantization described in the previous step is fairly invasive, but is required for backwards compatibility. For more stable future compatibility, implement the `dequantize` method on HFQuantizer. This method should be implemented [here](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/blob/37974267efefe020168ff27081fbab8bbce04720/src/transformers/quantizers/quantizer_compressed_tensors.py#L82-L85). Modify HFQuantizer to always decompress models if CT version is greater than 0.13 [here](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/blob/37974267efefe020168ff27081fbab8bbce04720/src/transformers/quantizers/quantizer_compressed_tensors.py#L82-L85).

candidates.title: RFC: Add Intel AutoRound Quantization Algorithm Support

labels.name: nvfp4
labels.description: For any PR / issue related to NVFP4 support

labels.name: wNa16

candidates.body:
Hi, here is the INC team from Intel.  Thank you for developing this amazing project!

Our team has developed **AutoRound**, a novel tuning-based quantization algorithm that delivers state-of-the-art accuracy with low tuning cost and no extra inference overhead. The key features are listed below:

- **Superior Accuracy:** Achieves leading performance across various scenarios, including very low bits (2-3 bits).
- **Multiple Data Types:** Effective for a variety of data types (W4A16, MXFP8, MXFP4, FP8, NVFP4, etc.).
- **Broad Model Support:** Validated on both Large Language Models (LLMs) and Vision-Language Models (VLMs).
- **Advanced Mixed-Precision:** Supports layer-wise mixed-bit quantization and automatic bit-width search.
- **Flexible Tuning:** Offers a configurable tuning space to balance tuning cost and accuracy goals.

 For more detailed information, please refer to our [paper](https://aclanthology.org/2024.findings-emnlp.662.pdf), and [GitHub repository](https://github.com/intel/auto-round/).

We propose integrating AutoRound into LLM Compressor to provide users with a simple, high-accuracy quantization option.

### The key Idea of AutoRound

AutoRound quantizes a given tensor by introducing three trainable parameters (`V`, α and β) to adjust the rounding value and clipping range. For a given transformers model, AutoRound quantizes the decoder block one by one, using block-wise output reconstruction error as loss to train these parameters.


![autoround_overview](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/bec1a573-f091-4b46-9dce-0302022746b3)

### Integration Proposal

AutoRound is already integrated into popular LLM ecosystems such as [Transformers](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/quantization/auto_round), [vLLM](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/features/quantization/auto_round.html), [SGLang](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/10153) and [TorchAO](https://github.com/pytorch/ao/tree/main/torchao/prototype/autoround).  For LLM Compressor, we proposed two integration options as below:

#### Option 1. A New `modifier` for AutoRound (Recommend)

This approach integrates AutoRound as a new modifier within LLM Compressor. Specifically, we propose creating an `AutoRoundModifier` that wraps the AutoRound algorithm, delegating the actual tuning logic to the [intel/auto-round](https://github.com/intel/auto-round) library. 
This method provides a lightweight, maintainable integration that directly leverages the AutoRound library while aligning perfectly with LLM Compressor's modifier architecture.


![option1](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/a1c7ebbf-74e0-420e-b83f-3104cedada4a)
(Modified from deepwiki https://deepwiki.com/vllm-project/llm-compressor/)

The initial design and potential code changes are as follows:

```python
# LLM Compressor/src/llmcompressor/modifiers/quantization/autoround/core.py

class AutoRoundModifier(Modifier, QuantizationMixin):

    def on_event(self, state: State, event: Event, **kwargs):
        if event.type_ == EventType.CALIBRATION_EPOCH_START:
            if not self.started_:
                self.on_start(state, None)

        if event.type_ == EventType.SEQUENTIAL_EPOCH_END:
            self.compress_modules()

        if event.type_ == EventType.CALIBRATION_EPOCH_END:
            self.compress_modules()

            if not self.ended_:
                self.on_end(state, None)

    def compress_modules(self):
        """
        Apply AutoRound tuning to a single decoding layer.
        This method delegates actual quantization to the AutoRound, 
        and updates the layer’s weights, scales, and zero points accordingly.
        """
        # TODO: Integrate with external tuning API.
        # Example (pseudo, TBD):
        #     tuned_layer = autoround.quant_block(decoding_layer, config=self.config)
        #     self._update_layer(decoding_layer, tuned_layer)
        pass
```

#### Option 2. Introduce a New Pipeline Wrapping Intel Neural Compressor (INC)

AutoRound is already implemented in [Intel/neural-compressor](https://github.com/intel/neural-compressor). INC supports popular model compression techniques across mainstream deep learning frameworks, including PyTorch, TensorFlow, and Jax (planned for the near future).
In this option, we propose introducing a new `pipeline` to wrap INC. This approach would allow us to leverage INC's framework abstraction infrastructure, paving the way for supporting more frameworks in the future.
![option2](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/3a8526b1-a2bf-4e3d-812e-7395b6a39f9c)
(Modified from deepwiki https://deepwiki.com/vllm-project/llm-compressor/)


```python
# llm-compressor/src/llmcompressor/pipelines/inc/pipeline.py

@CalibrationPipeline.register("inc")
class INCPipeline(CalibrationPipeline):
    @staticmethod
    def __call__(
        model: torch.nn.Module,
        dataloader: DataLoader,
        dataset_args: Union["DatasetArguments", None],
    ):
        """
        Applies the INC calibration procedure.
        """
        dispatch_for_generation(model)  # basic dispatch is identical to generation
        model_device = get_execution_device(model)

        from neural_compressor.torch.quantization import prepare, convert
        inc_config = prepare_autoround_config(...)
        model = prepare(model, inc_config)
        # apply calibration
        for batch in tqdm.tqdm(dataloader, desc="Calibrating"):
            model(**batch)
        model = convert(model)

```

#### Comparison Between Two Options:
| Item                        | Option 1: AutoRound Modifier                              | Option 2: INC Pipeline                                   |
| :-------------------------- | :-------------------------------------------------------- | :----------------------------------------------------------- |
| Architectural Alignment | Native fit within LLM Compressor’s modifier paradigm.     | A new pipeline                                                 |
| Dependencies            | Only requires `auto-round`library.               | Entire INC toolkit and its dependencies.                        |
| Implementation Effort   |  Utilizes existing APIs with localized modifications. | Requires designing a new pipeline and mapping configurations. |
| Model Scope    | Focus on LLMs and VLMs                       | Broader, including LLMs, VLMs, and models from other domains like CV. |
| Framework Support       | Focus PyTorch    | Multi-framework: Inherits INC’s PyTorch/TF/JAX support.      |

Based on the comparison, we recommend going with Option 1 to add AutoRound support. Please feel free to comment on the flow mentioned above or suggest additional approaches:). Thank you in advance!

candidates.body:
I suspect some of the quant I create are suboptimal, it would be extremely helpful to have a way to evaluate how well the quantized model reproduce the original's raw probability distribution before any sampler.

Hence it would be helpful to have a tool that reports KL-divergence with base model, KLD(A, B) and KLD(B, A) since KL divergence is asymmetric.

candidates.title: [Help Wanted] Update models used in tests

labels.name: good first issue
labels.description: A good first issue for users wanting to contribute

candidates.body:
Some of the models we use in tests have grown outdated. Others are larger than necessary for the nature of the test. Many of our per-commit / nightly tests are also focused on ensuring the model can be compressed/run but don't test the quality of the compressed model. This means we can use a very small "smoke llm" that has the same architecture as a regular llm but is too small to produce real outputs.

#1833 does exactly this to replace one of the test models with a 6-layer llm with less than 0.5M weights. However, there are also other models (such as `TinyLlama/TinyLlama-1.1B-intermediate-step-1431k-3T`) that could potentially be replaced.

# Goals
1. Update tests to use more modern models
2. Reduce the runtime of tests (particularly the transformers check test)

# Suggested Approach
1. Determine the most common test models in use in the repo's tests.
2. Determine if these models could be replaced with a dummy "smoke llm" based on how they are used in tests
3. (If possible) evaluate which models/tests account for the greatest amount of test runtime
4. Replace models in tests with a smaller/newer model from the same model family (or a smoke model designed for that purpose)

candidates.title: [RFC]: MR-GPTQ (GPTQ+NVFP4)
candidates.body:
A new paper came out that tailors GPTQ to MXFP4 and NVFP4 storage format:
- https://arxiv.org/pdf/2509.23202

> The recent hardware-accelerated microscaling 4-bit floating-point formats such as MXFP4 and NVFP4, supported on NVIDIA and AMD GPUs, promise to revolutionize large language model (LLM) inference. Yet, their practical benefits remain unproven. We present the first comprehensive study of MXFP4 and NVFP4 for post-training quantization, revealing gaps between their promise and real-world performance. Our analysis shows that state-of-the-art methods struggle with FP4, due to two key issues: (1) NVFP4's small group size provably neutralizes traditional outlier mitigation techniques; (2) MXFP4's power-of-two scale quantization severely degrades accuracy due to high induced error. To bridge this gap, we introduce Micro-Rotated-GPTQ (MR-GPTQ), a variant of the classic GPTQ quantization algorithm that tailors the quantization process to FP4's unique properties, by using block-wise Hadamard transforms and format-specific optimizations. We support our proposal with a set of high-performance GPU kernels that enable the MR-GPTQ format with negligible overhead, by rotation fusion into the weights, and fast online computation of the activations. This leads to speedups vs. FP16 of up to 3.6x layer-wise, and 2.2x end-to-end on NVIDIA B200, and of 6x layer-wise and 4x end-to-end on RTX5090. Our extensive empirical evaluation demonstrates that MR-GPTQ matches or outperforms state-of-the-art accuracy, significantly boosting MXFP4, to the point where it can near the accuracy that of NVFP4. We conclude that, while FP4 is not an automatic upgrade over INT4, format-specialized methods like MR-GPTQ can unlock a new frontier of accuracy-performance trade-offs. 

The models are supported in vLLM since https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/24440 and reference quantization framework is https://github.com/IST-DASLab/FP-Quant

candidates.title: About lora finetuning of 2:4 sparse and sparse quant models
candidates.body:
I would like to thank for a great repo. 

I have been testing the newly released sparse quant models and was amazed by speedup in both latency and throughput.
I just have some doubts regarding finetuning of 2:4 sparse models.

From what i understood, the model is first sparsified and then fully trained on some data to create sparse llama base model.
As this is not instruction tuned, we do another finetuning on instruction data (which is much smaller). But this still takes as much memory but lesser time. 

The recipe provided in the examples, starts with a dense model and does sparsification based on calibration data. Then fine tuning is applied to create the sparse model to regain accuracy. 

I would like to know if we can start with a sparse base model (like Sparse Llama 3.1 8B), and create a lora adapter using custom dataset. There can also be sparsity speedup for training lora adapters, is this possible? This would take a lot memory than finetuning step after sparsification.

Does this make sense, assuming VLLM supports serving sparse models with lora?  
Can all this be also applied to sparse + w4a16 models to get Qlora +sparsity training and inference?

I would like to contribute if anyone points me in the right direction.

Thanks
Arun

    return {key: torch.tensor(value) for key, value in batch[0].items()}

    targets="Linear",

)

)

import base64

dampening_frac=0.01

    # preprocess

    max_seq_length=MAX_SEQUENCE_LENGTH,
    num_calibration_samples=NUM_CALIBRATION_SAMPLES,
    trust_remote_code_model=True,

    output_dir=SAVE_DIR,

)

candidates.title: Speed Comparison: BitLinear and nn.Linear
candidates.body:
Hello,

I measured the time of your BitLinear and BitLinearBitBLAS against nn.Linear, and it seems that the time for smaller input_features and out_features is slower than nn.Linear. Is there a solution for this?

I used the quant_utils from your BitNet integration: https://github.com/microsoft/BitBLAS/blob/main/integration/BitNet/utils_quant.py

My GPU is NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3090

```
import time
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
from torch.autograd import Variable

# from bitlinear import BitLinear, BitLinearBitBLAS
from utils_quant import BitLinear, BitLinearBitBLAS

# Function to measure computation time
def measure_time(layer, input_tensor, num_runs=100):
    with torch.no_grad():
        # Warm up
        for _ in range(100): ## 100
            _ = layer(input_tensor)
        
        start_time = time.time()
        for _ in range(num_runs):
            _ = layer(input_tensor)
        torch.cuda.synchronize()  #### new
        end_time = time.time()
        
        avg_time = (end_time - start_time) / num_runs
    return avg_time

# # # Test parameters
input_features = 512
output_features = 256
batch_size = 8

# input_features = 1024
# output_features = 512
# batch_size = 32

# input_features = 10240
# output_features = 5120
# batch_size = 32

# input_features = 20480
# output_features = 10240
# batch_size = 32


# Create random input tensor
input_tensor = torch.randn(batch_size, input_features).cuda()

# Initialize layers
nn_linear_layer = nn.Linear(input_features, output_features).cuda()
bit_linear_layer = BitLinear(input_features, output_features).cuda()

bitblas_linear_layer = BitLinearBitBLAS.from_bit_linear(bit_linear_layer)

# Measure computation time
num_runs = 100
nn_linear_time = measure_time(nn_linear_layer, input_tensor, num_runs)
bit_linear_time = measure_time(bit_linear_layer, input_tensor, num_runs)
bitblas_linear_time = measure_time(bitblas_linear_layer, input_tensor, num_runs)

print('input_features, output_features, batch_size: ', input_features, output_features, batch_size)
print(f"Average computation time for nn.Linear: {nn_linear_time * 1000:.4f} ms")
print(f"Average computation time for fp32 simulated BitLinear: {bit_linear_time * 1000:.4f} ms")
print(f"Average computation time Bitblas BitLinear: {bitblas_linear_time * 1000:.4f} ms")


```

Here are the testing results:

```

Thanks for your reply in advance.

        self.create_bitblas_weights()

    def _get_or_create_bitblas_operator(self, config, enable_tuning):
        if global_operator_cache.size() == 0:
            global_operator_cache.load_from_database(BITBLAS_DATABASE_PATH, BITBLAS_TARGET)

        bitblas_matmul = global_operator_cache.get(config)
        if bitblas_matmul is None:
            # should disable tuning for the first time because we may require loading bitblas operator from database.
            bitblas_matmul = bitblas.Matmul(config, target=BITBLAS_TARGET, enable_tuning=False)
            if enable_tuning:
                bitblas_matmul.hardware_aware_finetune(topk=20)
                global_operator_cache.add(config, bitblas_matmul)
                global_operator_cache.save_into_database(BITBLAS_DATABASE_PATH, BITBLAS_TARGET)
                print("BitBLAS Tuning done, appended operator to global_operator_cache.")
            else:
                print("BitBLAS Operator created.")
        else:
            print("BitBLAS Operator found in global_operator_cache.")
        return bitblas_matmul
    
    def create_bitblas_weights(self):
        qweight = self.bitblas_matmul.transform_weight(self.weight)
        qweight = nn.Parameter(qweight, requires_grad=False)
        self.register_buffer("qweight", qweight)
    
    @torch.compile
    def activation_quant(self, x, num_bits=8):
        Qn = -(2**(num_bits - 1))
        Qp = 2**(num_bits - 1) - 1
        s = Qp / x.abs().max(dim=-1, keepdim=True).values.clamp(min=1e-5)
        result = (x * s).round().clamp(Qn, Qp)
        return result.type(torch.int8), s

    @torch.compile
    def post_quant_process(self, input, si, sw):
        out = input / si
        out = out / sw
        return out
    
    def simple_forward(self, x):
        w = self.weight
        w_quant = w.to(torch.bfloat16)
        x_quant, x_scale = self.activation_quant(x, self.input_bits)
        y = self.post_quant_process(F.linear(x_quant.to(torch.bfloat16), w_quant) , x_scale, self.weight_scale)

candidates.title: Any plans to release the ternary vLLM kernels used in the whitepaper evals?
candidates.body:
The whitepaper evals ran on EvalScope + vLLM on H100, so ternary vLLM kernels exist internally. The only public CUDA path today is the llama.cpp fork. Is a public release (or a timeline for one) planned? And if not, would you bless or seed a community port? The fork's CUDA kernels plus vLLM's quant-backend interface look like a tractable bridge, and I suspect several of us would pitch in.

Why it matters, quantified (RTX 5060 Ti 16 GB, from the community-benchmarks submission in PR #98 and the linked repo):

- Batch 1, ternary on the fork: 44 t/s decode. Excellent; it beats a 12B running on vLLM with speculation on the same card (26 t/s).
- Under concurrency the picture flips: at 8 streams the fork's slot batching reaches ~91 t/s aggregate but TTFT p95 degrades to ~25 s, while the smaller model on vLLM holds TTFT p95 ~0.3 s flat at the same concurrency. The serving stack, not the model, decides who wins the multi-stream seat.
- The fork also cannot combine the DSpark drafter with more than one slot, so speculation and concurrency are mutually exclusive today.

In short: Ternary Bonsai currently loses production deployments it would otherwise win on quality and VRAM, to smaller models with better serving. vLLM kernels (continuous batching, paged KV, prefix caching, plus speculation) on 16 GB consumer cards would close that gap.

Happy to be a first tester on consumer Blackwell (sm_120) and to contribute the benchmark harness: https://github.com/Astezelex/bonsai-27b-16gb-bench

candidates.title: ROCm: Q2_0 ternary GGUF models fail to load (valid GGUFv3)
candidates.body:
## Environment
- GPU: Radeon 8060S (gfx1151, Strix Halo)
- ROCm 7.2.4
- Build: Bonsai-demo llama.cpp build-rocm-test

## Issue
Ternary Q2_0 quantized GGUF models fail to load with `main: error: failed to load model` despite being valid GGUFv3 files:

Files tested:
- `Ternary-Bonsai-8B-Q2_0.gguf` (GGUFv3, 399 tensors)
- `Ternary-Bonsai-27B-Q2_0.gguf` (GGUFv3, 851 tensors)
- `Ternary-Bonsai-1.7B-Q2_0.gguf` (GGUFv3, 310 tensors)

These are all confirmed valid GGUFv3 format. The F16 version of the same model (`Ternary-Bonsai-1.7B-F16.gguf`) loads and runs fine.

## Impact
Cannot run ternary-quantized models which are significantly smaller (460 MB vs 3.2 GB for the 1.7B) and would give much higher decode speeds. The community benchmarks show 231 tok/s on Q1_0 quant vs our 49.7 tok/s on F16 — that's 4.6x faster decode.

## Suspected Cause
Missing ternary quantization kernel support (likely TQ1_0 / TQ2_0 format) in the non-PrismML build. The PrismML prism branch has Q1_0 DP4A kernels that are not present in this build.
